subsubtopic: JOB SECURITY FOR RURAL CONTRACT AGENTS-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT TO MAKE CORRECT DECISIONS
speechtext:
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, 1 called the attention of the House on
February 9, 1988

the unacceptable situation Canada Post rural contract agents must live with. At the time, I described the situation faced by Mr. Ronald Laliberte, from Hawkesbury, in my Glengarry- Prescott-Russell riding, who has been a rural contract agent for the Post Office for over 30 years and who, because of some Canada Post procedure, could find himself without a job in spite of his long and loyal services. For almost two years now,
5,000	rural contract agents are faced with the same dilemma as Mr. Laliberte when they see their contracts extended without any guarantee from Canada Post.
The Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation should make the required decisions by making it possible for rural contract agents to renew their contracts without jeopardizing their jobs. Why should a Canadian citizen who has been a Post Office employee for 30 years have to make a bid each year to keep his job? Mr. Speaker, such an attitude is altogether unacceptable, and the Government of Canada should protect the job of rural contract agents in this country.
SUPREME COURT DECIStON-EFFECT ON UNBORN BABIES

Mr. Speaker, the recent Supreme Court ruling overturning Section 251 of the Criminal Code leaves all unborn babies defenceless in their mother's womb.
Did you know that four days after conception sex can be determined under a special microscope? Or that 24 to 25 days after conception the heart begins to beat and pump its own blood? Or that 43 days after conception brain waves can be detected? Or that 30 days after conception, foundations of the brain, spinal cord, nerves and sense organs are completely formed?
All of the following occur even before the mother knows she is pregnant: nerves and muscles begin working together; lips become sensitive to touch and the shape of the body is unmistakably human and possesses all the internal organs of an adult. In fact, the stomach produces digestive juices, the liver manufactures red blood cells, and the kidney eliminates uric acid from the body. Even the legs, arms, fingers and toes have already been formed. From this point on the only changes will be in size and sophistication of use of the unborn's parts.
Under Canadian law there is no cut-off date after which abortions may not be performed. It is incumbent upon Parliament to exhibit moral leadership in establishing laws to stop the killing of approximately 100,000 babies in their mothers' wombs each year.

subtopic: S. O. 21 HOUSING PLIGHT OF HOMELESS-INCREASED GOVERNMENT FUNDING URGED
S. O. 21 HOUSING PLIGHT OF HOMELESS-INCREASED GOVERNMENT FUNDING URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Ottawa, and in every other Canadian city, there are men and women without shelter. They sleep in the streets, on park benches, in abandoned buildings, and under bridges. The number of people chronically without shelter is still relatively small but nonetheless significant, and the fact it is increasing is alarming.
During 1987, the United Nations International Year of Shelter for the Homeless, the Canada Council on Social Development produced a comprehensive study of homelessness in Canada. Its recommendations, ranging from a complete review of the Canada Assistance Plan, expanding social programs and developing new ones, to establishing national objectives for increasing the supply of low-cost housing, and viewing housing construction as a vehicle to put people back to work, have the potential to go a long way. What is needed now is a strong commitment by the federal Government and provincial Governments to provide the money and support necessary to implement these recommendations.
The International Year of Shelter for the Homeless has passed, but the problem will persist until we can find the political will to change it. I urge the Government to meet that challenge, and there is no better place to do it than when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brings his Budget forward tomorrow. He could increase the funding allocation for the homeless then.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative northern defence policy of providing optimum protection and sovereign control at a reasonable price is compelling in its good sense and logic. The NDP policy of surrendering the nation to the first Russian soldier to step off his skidoo might appeal to a few. What makes no sense at all is the Liberal policy outlined in Vancouver by their Party Leader (Mr. Turner) on the weekend.
The Liberals would spend billions of dollars on diesel submarines completely incapable of operating under the ice, thereby abandoning any semblance of Canadian Arctic sovereignty to the Americans. Using the same logic, maybe the Liberals would want to replace our tanks with Roman catapults, equip our infantry with longbows, and reintroduce the cavalry.

February 9, 1988

subsubtopic: ISRAEL-DISTURBANCES IN GAZA AND WEST BANK-UNITED STATES PEACE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a sense of unease that I watch the struggle, feel the hostility, and sense the futility on all sides of the disturbances in the Gaza and West Bank. The confrontations have created a dangerously unstable situation which causes serious concern for many people in Canada and around the world.
Since 1945, 150 regional wars have caused 20 million casualties, mostly civilian men, women and children, and forced many people to seek refuge from violence and oppression. While some of these disputes in the Middle East have been settled, the same is not true in the Gaza and West Bank despite many concrete attempts to resolve the situation. Recent events demonstrate the need for direct negotiations towards a peaceful resolution of the conflict. Valuable time is being lost in the search for a just and lasting peace that recognizes Israel within secure boundaries and responds to the aspirations of the Palestinians.
Restoration of order is a necessary first step. While no army or police force in the world should have to forgo its right to self-defence, it remains true that human rights know no boundaries and must be respected. I urge all parties to refrain from further aggression and to work towards an environment in which a negotiated settlement can be found. The U.S. peace plan may be such a starting point. It is an initiative worth serious consideration. Let this not be another tragedy of lost opportunity.

subsubtopic: SENATE DELAY IN PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past two weeks Canadians have been skilfully manipulated by Mahmoud Mohammad, the terrorist convicted in Greece of attacking an Israeli jet in which there was a loss of life. Flanked by his family, this individual told Canadians that he was rehabilitated, and gave a hazy account of the terrorist attack.
It has now been proven that Mr. Mohammad's account of the incident was false. However, there is a major principle at stake here. The principle is what this individual represents. Terrorists have no compassion, pity, or remorse. Their only aim is terror, to be achieved by any means they have at their disposal. Any human being is a potential target for these cowardly people for they only prey on those who cannot defend themselves.
These individuals have been responsible for thousands of innocent deaths throughout the world. They are responsible for the unprecedented security now enforced at all points of departure. Yet this individual is making a mockery of our immigration system. While the Government has passed C-55 and C-84 to control this abuse, the Senate continues to stall its process. 1 call on the other place to act before more criminals enter Canada.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Assistant Deputy Registrar General, Mr. Kingsley, claimed that the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) arrangements do not constitute a potential conflict of interest.
I would assert that this is not the case. By his actions the Prime Minister is in a natural conflict. As this House knows, we are studying Bill C-79, an Act to amend the Canada Elections Act. Negotiations are ongoing regarding the disclosure of the financial status of local political Party associations and a fuller disclosure of the financial transactions of the central Parties.
Ordinary Canadians deserve to know what is happening with money provided by rebates and tax credits. They wish to know what the federal Parties are doing with this money. The New Democratic Party has always been in favour of open disclosure. Despite our attempts during negotiations with the other Parties, all we have been given in the Bill is a voluntary disclosure of the financial status of local association funds. This is simply not good enough. We must either eliminate this farce, or make the legislation binding and enforceable.
It seems that working Canadians cannot expect the Prime Minister and his Party to be in favour of the disclosure of his Party's financial records when it includes information that is embarrassing to himself. Mr. Speaker, ordinary Canadians, through the tax rebate system and the tax credit system, are paying a lot of money to the PC Fund. We deserve to know and should have legislation to ensure that that information is available to the public.

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR MEASURES TO PROTECT UNBORN CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court of Canada has struck down the abortion law as breaching the Charter of Rights. However, the court has not said that the Charter gives a woman the right to an abortion. Rather, it
February 9, 1988

has said that, although Section 251 of the Criminal Code breaches the Charter, Parliament does have the power to enact legislation restricting abortion and protecting the unborn child.
As one of my constituents said, we did not elect the Supreme Court to govern Canada. Surely, with due respect to Parliament as a mechanism of Canadian democracy, we could reenact Section 251 of the Criminal Code as well as invoking the provisions of Section 33 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to provide protection to the unborn child pending a permanent solution to this very pressing problem.

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the natural reaction of the Government when facing a controversial issue like abortion is to sit on the fence and avoid falling into either camp. That is exactly what it is doing now.
Last week the highest court in the land ruled that women have a right to decide on the choices affecting their own reproduction. As a result, the country is in a state of confusion. Abortion is now supposed to be legal but most provinces have done nothing to come to terms with this reality.
The tidal wave has swept across the country and the Conservative Government is refusing to clean up the chaos left behind. I ask the Government to start cleaning up, to start facing today's new reality. Canada is confused and needs direction.
When is the Conservative Government going to stop studying the document and start facing its responsibilities? When are Canadian women across Canada going to have equal access to all services and options regarding reproduction? When is the federal Government going to give the provinces and the people of Canada some leadership on this issue?
I ask the Government at least to recognize that women have more choice today than they did last week and that access to all choices and options concerning reproduction must be guaranteed. It is time that the Government started cleaning up the confusion.

SOCIAL PROGRAMS-ABSENCE OF REAL POLICY IN CONSERVATIVE PARTY FOR YOUTH-OUTLOOK FOR FUTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an article which appeared in the newspaper Le Devoir has raised a very important matter for the future of the country, more specifically dealing with young Canadians.
This question is raised at a time when the various governments are considering the rationalization of funds invested in social programs, including higher contributions of workers to various pension funds.

February 9, 1988

Mr. Speaker, 1988 marked the beginning of the twenty-sixth year since the erection of the Berlin Wall, first established in 1961 to seal off the Soviet sector from the rest of Berlin.
The Berlin Wall remains an ugly and hated symbol of the division of Germany and the German people, and is a monument to the distrust and paranoia of the communist regime. While we struggle to deal with the many and vast differences between East and West, the tragedy that is the Berlin Wall should not be allowed to slip into obscurity.
The Wall epitomizes the difference between East and West and defines the reality of the Soviet Bloc, a vast prison from which there is little chance of escape. It has divided a nation and a people, and must be demolished. Not to do so would be a betrayal of the many brave individuals who have lost their lives attempting to scale its treacherous walls.
I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Government of Canada to use all available measures to maintain pressure on the Soviet Union until this barricade to freedom is dismantled, never to be erected again.

subtopic: MEDICAL RECORDS-ABSENCE OF UNIFORM REGULATIONS GOVERNING RETENTION
MEDICAL RECORDS-ABSENCE OF UNIFORM REGULATIONS GOVERNING RETENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at present no federal legislation regulates the length of time medical records must be retained, nor does legislation require doctors or hospitals to release medical records or test results to patients.
When doctors do not release this kind of information to their patients and files are eventually discarded, a patient is left with no records at all.
The need for these records is becoming increasingly evident. Many illnesses take considerable time for diagnosis and medical histories have a bearing on the health of descendants and other family members. Our increasingly mobile population adds to the difficulty of updating medical records.
At present each province and territory has jurisdiction over its own Health Ministry regulations on the issue of the retention of medical records. These run the gamut from no regulations at all in Newfoundland, Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories, to Prince Edward Island which retains records for 50 years if microfilmed. Other provinces retain them for varying lengths of time, from five years in Quebec to 30 years in Manitoba.
I urge the Government to work with the provinces to develop a consistent policy across the country on this important matter.

He will know that his Minister of Indian Affairs recently announced the provision of sizeable aid, some $9.5 million, from the Western Diversification Fund for the establishment of a Japanese owned pulp mill to be located in the Peace River district of northern Alberta. Be that as it may, the timber for use in this mill is to be cut from lands which are subject to the yet unsettled Lubicon Indian land claim.
How can it be reconciled that the Minister takes action of this kind as Minister responsible for the Western Diversification Fund at the same time as he has constitutional trust obligations to protect the interests of Indian bands? Is there not here a very classic case of conflict of interest?

The Hon. Member puts that as a fact in the preamble of his question and that is not necessarily agreed upon.
The Hon. Member knows that cutting rights and provincial jurisdiction flow from that as well. The judgment which he made in his concluding statement does not necessarily follow from the facts, and neither does it follow that the conclusion he drew is correct.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister takes much unto himself when he denies that there is any conflict. I think that is a very large constitutional question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege relates to information which came before the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs this morning before which the Hon. E. Davie Fulton appeared as a witness. As was pointed out by the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), all three Parties have now joined in urging bilateral negotiations with Mr. Fulton as the negotiator on the Lubicon claim.
However, during the committee hearing we learned that yesterday the Government of Alberta made a joint announcement with the federal Government through the office of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) who also handles western diversification. An announcement was made of plans to fund jointly the $500 million pulp mill in Peace River on lands that are, at least in part, those lands in question presently being negotiated with the Lubicon Band.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) just indicated to the House that the lands involved with the Daishowa company are not lands overlying the Lubicon claim. However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare may have inadvertently misled the House in that the Forest Minister for Alberta, Mr. Fjordbotten, has now confirmed that the lands involved, some 11,200 square miles of land, do in fact overlie the Lubicon claim and the lands that are presently being negotiated.
Privilege-Mr. Fulton

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. If my hon. friend has some way of proving that it is something on which the House should use its time, then I suggest he should come to that point of his argument very quickly and we can then listen to the rest of it.

speechtext:
I have no difficulty with that, Mr. Speaker, I was just coming to that very point.
The fact of the matter is that the Minister of Indian Affairs is responsible for the negotiations which are presently high centred in relation to the Lubicon claim. The same Minister is responsible for the Western Diversification Fund, and yesterday he made an announcement of an expenditure of $9.5 million which now removes those very lands that were supposedly being negotiated in good faith.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is the only Minister of the federal Crown who holds a specific trust relationship with a specific group of Canadians, that being the first citizens, the first nations of this country. These 11,200 square miles of the Province of Alberta have been transferred without public hearings and without tendering. The Minister who is now funding the Diashowa project, the same Minister who was supposedly dealing in good faith with the Lubicon Band has, in my humble view, involved himself and the good offices of the Ministry of Aboriginal Affairs in a breach of trust. I think it is a very simple and clear-cut case in which the federal Crown has not lived up to its responsibilities to the Lubicon people. This has been carried forward in reports by the Ombudsman of Alberta and various groups including the World Council of Churches and the United Nations.
My friend, the Member for Cochrane-Superior, has several additional points which he would like to make. However, 1 think this is a prima facie case of a Minister of the Crown with specific constitutional responsibilities and specific legislative responsibilities in relation to the first citizens which are not being upheld and have now been specifically violated by an expenditure under another part of a portfolio held by the same Minister.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should advise Hon. Members that there was an Hon. Member on his feet when the matter was adjourned. I have looked for him and he is not here. I think I should appropriately recognize the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I in no way wanted to intrude upon the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie). 1 look forward to what he has to say as I did on many occasions when he held high office in the City of Toronto.
I have taken part in many debates on constitutional matters. During the course of my public life I have seen some important breakthroughs. I am very proud that I had the honour, when I was the Minister of Justice, to share the responsibility for piloting the original Bill on the Official Languages Act in 1969. Consequently, you can understand my pleasure in being able to rise to take part in this debate on the second reading of Bill C-72, the up-dated version of the Official Languages Act.
Some talk about state sanctioned bilingualism as if it were born with Bill C-72, or with the Meech Lake Accord last year, or with Mr. Trudeau's 1982 Constitutional Act. The fact is that bilingualism began with the British North America Act of 1867, Section 133. Admittedly, that was only a parliamentary and judicial regime applicable only to Ontario and Quebec, to federal and Quebec parliaments and our courts of justice.
By the early 1960s it was still so meek and mild a regime that when I arrived in this place in 1962 the main aspects of bilingualism being discussed on the floor of the House were bilingual family allowance cheques, bilingual menus in the parliamentary restaurant, dollar bills, and in eloquent terms I can still remember the late Real Caouette, Leader of the Social Credit Party, complaining about the lack of bilingualism on TransCanada Airline planes, later Air Canada.
As a Member from Montreal at the time, for the now disappeared riding of St. Lawrence-St. George, I felt as dismayed, indeed as outraged, as my other Quebec colleagues.
Andre Laurendeau wrote in his famous letter of January 20, 1962, that became the starting point for the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission:
[ Translation]
"Issuing bilingual cheques is too little, too late, considering the present aspirations of French Canadians".

He understood well the mood of that age. As a result of that type of persuasion, the persuasion of Liberals around Mr. Pearson, particularly Maurice Lamontagne, Mr. Pearson brought in the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, known familiarly as the Laurendeau-Dunton commission.
From 1964 to 1970 the commission issued six reports which were to revolutionalize Canadian thinking on the subject. The preliminary report called for two equal official languages in Canada. Another report called for the protection of minority language rights across the country. The third report called for the guarantee of the rights of public servants to work in their own language and culture.
The Bill we are discussing today reflects the spirit of Laurendeau-Dunton as it has been revived and nourished by several commissions and committees.

I have the honour of sitting in the House with my old friend, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), and I would like to pay tribute to his work and to the role he has played and continues to play in promoting bilingualism in the Public Service and protecting language minorities in the provinces. I don't want to embarrass him, but it is always a pleasure to praise my colleagues from time to time.
During the past 20 years, the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier worked first for the school boards here in Ottawa and subsequently in the House of Commons, but always spurring governments onward, both Liberals and Conservatives.
He did so especially from 1980 to 1984, as Chairman of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. He still does today as a Member of the Standing Joint Committee, and he has had considerable input in some of the concepts and mechanisms contained in Bill C-72.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier is a typical example of the Member who believes in a goal, a mission, and who manages to get his message across, despite the slowness of our procedures and the often crushing pressure of the executive on the business of the House.
1 thought the expressions of appreciation that came to him from all sides of the House during the debate on January 25 were well deserved.
February 9, 1988



Let me make three points on the principles of this Bill. In advertising terms, the time is right, the subject is right and the content is right. Some commentators, particularly on the other side of the House, say that we do not need the Bill. They suggest that because there is peace on the language front now we should let sleeping dogs lie rather than arouse the passions of the country or provoke old antagonisms. In other words, why do we not wait for a crisis?
We have done that too often before. We waited too long before bringing in the Bill finally in 1969. We waited too long to patriate our Constitution in 1982. We waited too long to bring Quebec fully into Confederation as we have attempted to do in the Constitutional Accord. Goodness knows that we have not really set our mind on reforming the Senate, something I hope to live long enough to see reformed-I would like to see an elected Senate.
There is a difference between prudence and procrastination. Prudence gets there eventually, procrastination never does. We are fortunate that there is no major linguistic conflict nationally at the present time, even though there are several regional and serious difficulties in language. That is why I believe that now the time is right to proceed to consolidate and enhance the Official Languages Act. Now is the time to weave in the many advances made since 1969 to keep the Act abreast of a changing mood and a positive tolerance in Canada. Therefore, the time is right.
Second, the subject is right. Some may be surprised to hear me speak about this Bill as a constitutional matter. Let me remind them and Members of the House that the Constitution is more than the separation or division of powers. The Constitution now includes our rights and liberties and provides for the equality of the two languages we speak.
The subject of Bill C-72 on the Official Languages Act is right for another reason. We passed a major constitutional Act in 1982 which includes a Charter of Rights enshrining language equality. Section 16 of the Charter states:
English and French are the official languages of Canada and have equality
of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all institutions of the
Parliament and the Government of Canada.
Through Sections 16 to 23 of the Charter a whole new institutional bilingualism regime is built in general terms and enshrined. Those sections cover Parliament, the administration, the courts, minority language system. Now some flesh must be placed on those bones. We cannot proclaim equality and then simply let it happen by accident. We must adjust our laws to accepted constitutional principles. The laws of this country must accord with the Constitution. That is a primary impetus behind bringing this law up to date.
Another major principle will be proclaimed when the Meech Lake Accord becomes the law of the land. According to the Constitutional Accord, English-French duality as a fundamental characteristic of our country will be proclaimed. My Party is in agreement with that. Some of my colleagues have had
Official Languages Act
problems with the second leg of the principle, the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society. I want to remind everyone in the House that this Party, in its resolution in November, 1986, by a majority of 85 per cent, approved the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society, not as a constitutional innovation but merely as a recognition of the fact that Quebec is unique and distinct, having been the only province speaking French in its majority and having a different system of law, different collective psychology and history.
There has never been any hesitation on the question of duality. My Party has been a perennial promoter of that concept since 1867. I have read some historians who say that we even invented it.
Those words in the 1982 Charter and the Meech Lake Accord must now be given flesh, teeth and specific meaning. That is what Bill C-72 does and that is why, once again, my Party is willing to support the Government against the attack of its right flank. It may be overly generous on our part electorally, but we are not about to abandon one of our deepest traditions, the promotion of national unity, identity and equality of our two languages, merely to score some political points on the floor of the House.
I leave to the Government benches their responsibility in bringing their Members into line and ensuring that they do not retard further progress of this Bill.
[ Translation]
Third, the content is right. During the debate on January 25, when the Opposition-our Party-insisted that Bill C-72 be tabled in the House for second reading, some Government backbenchers asked, as if they had just invented the wheel, what the Liberal Party had done about institutional bilingualism between 1969 and 1984, when it was in power. Madam Speaker, ignorance is bliss.
One of the reasons why this Bill is acceptable to us and to a substantial majority of Canadians is that it is in our Party's tradition, which includes the 1969 Act, the experience we acquired from 1969 to 1984, the Parliamentary Resolution of 1973, the 1982 Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the proceedings of the Joint Committee on Official Languages, especially from 1980 to 1984 when it was led and chaired by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier).
Take, for instance, the right of public servants to work in their own language. That right was expressed for the first time by Mr. Pearson, together with the right of public servants occupying a position designated bilingual to receive language training. The right to choose one's language of work is implicit in Section 2 of the 1969 Act. It was the object of a parliamentary resolution in 1973 and the joint committee agreed that it was urgent to amend the legislation because it was ambiguous, as was confirmed by the many court rulings.
Among other things, Madam Speaker, that is what Bill C-72 does. Why is that possible? Because mentalities have evolved and because parliamentary, judicial, administrative

February 9, 1988
Official Languages Act
and academic bilingualism has progressed at both provincial and federal levels.
Madam Speaker, I regret to say that a monthly publication delivered across western Canada, Western Report, printed these words on its cover: If you cannot read this you cannot work for the federal Government. It appears in both languages.
The magazine, Western Report, is carried throughout our western provinces. It had on its latest front cover a sentence in French which read: "If you can't read this, you can't work for the federal Government". That is simply not true. That it should be written and widely distributed in the current climate of this country, I think, is a shame. The Government knows that is not true and it should be telling Canadians that it is not true. I hope the Secretary of State when he gets to his feet, will say so. The truth is that thousands of Canadians can read those lines in French because of the progress which has been made in the last 20 years.
In every major community in western Canada immersion courses in the French language are becoming more and more popular. In my riding of Vancouver Quadra we have 15 high schools. There are French immersion courses in each. I try to visit every one of those high schools and the students proudly put questions to me in French-probably to test my own French-which demonstrates that in Canada we can feel comfortable using the other language. The students look forward not only to becoming better Canadians by speaking the other language but by becoming part of the human race in a wider civilized scope while enjoying two of the greatest cultures ever brought forward by the mind and ingenuity of mankind. That is why the cover of that magazine is contrary to that spirit.
In fact those who cannot speak French can still work in the federal Government. Sixty per cent of all federal positions in the public service of Canada are designated unilingual English. Only 7 per cent are designated unilingual French. That is the truth. That is what western Canadians should know. That is what English speaking Canadians should know. The Government has the responsibility today to tell them the truth. Sixty per cent of all federal positions are designated unilingual English and only 7 per cent are designated unilingual French.

Madam Speaker, I said more about one aspect of the contents of the legislation, freedom of choice with respect to the language of work in the federal public service. A few years ago I had the same responsibility as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), namely to represent a national capital riding. So again I ask the question: What does Bill C-72 do? The answer is very clear. Basically the Bill consolidates, legalizes, and allows for regulations; exceptionally, it strengthens and extends the legislation of 1969.
What does it consolidate? First, the Official Languages Act of 1969; second, the 1973 resolution of the House of Commons in favour of free choice with respect to language of work and bilingual training; third, the right of the two linguistic groups to participate fully in the operations of the federal administration. It also consolidates the Constitution Act of 1982, whose sections 16 to 23 enshrined institutional bilingualism; the spirit of the Meech Lake Accord is consolidated, particularly concerning the Canadian duality; and finally all the experience acquired since 1969, since the existing Official Languages Act was adopted and in the implementation of the objectives of institutional bilingualism in all sectors: the parliamentary experience, the judicial experience, the administrative experience
What does this Bill do with regard to principles? Let us look at the essential. First and foremost, institutional or state bilingualism, as opposed to individual bilingualism which created for the Government a series of obligations under the 1969 legislation, will become now, due to the incorporation of the effects of Clause 16 of the 1982 Constitutional Act, not only a series of enforceable obligations for the Government, but also a series of rights for Canadian citizens. The supremacy of the Official Languages Act is confirmed and its content adapted to the 1982 Constitutional Reform.
Second, the equality of the official languages is now defined and applied to the federal Public Service, our courts of justice, and the protection of the linguistic minorities within the provinces. The choice as to the language of work, implicitly contained in the 1969 legislation, is now made explicit. So is the principle of full participation by members of our two linguistic communities. The promotion of these measures is now the responsibility of the Treasury Board and the Secretary of State. The Commissioner will enjoy extended powers. He will have the authority to get involved in proceedings instituted by individuals before the courts, or he might even institute such proceedings himself.
Third, the legislation will continue to evolve but it will have acquired much more precision and strength. Instead of being expressed by the Government's instructions or voluntary programs, it will be expressed through regulations dealing, for instance, with the language of work, full participation, the definition of a "major request", the function of the Treasury Board and that of the Secretary of State.
These regulations will be of tremendous importance. On occasion they will have as much importance as the Act itself. As parliamentarians, we do not hold the regulating process in high esteem, but the arbitrary process clearly has its drawbacks too. We will have to keep an eye on these regulations, demand their tabling in the House and their discussion in Committee. We will see to that as long as we sit in the Opposition and then again when we are the Government.
February 9, 1988

I had the honour of bringing in the Statutory Instruments Act which ensured that every regulation and every Order in Council promulgated by this executive responsible to this Parliament was published within a period appropriate to the occasion, giving the Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments Committee an opportunity to review those regulations and orders and render reports on them, and to ensure particularly that those orders were within the ambit of the power accorded by Parliament and not exceeding that ambit. Since the regulations under this Bill will have wide-ranging consequences, will fall within the ambit of the law but will render more precise the application of the law, it is important that Members of the House exercise their surveillance and monitoring function with the usual aptitude and persistence.
I said that the time is right, Madam Speaker, the subject is right, and the content is right. I urge all Members of the House to support the Bill, and send it to committee. There may be amendments proposed. As one who has the honour of holding a seat in western Canada, I particularly appeal to those Members who may have some reservations about the Bill to recognize the progress we have made since the early 1960s in recognizing the dual nature of our linguistic heritage, the understanding that that gives to us and the tolerance that it reflects, which make our federal system work.
Canadians from coast to coast and people from around the world will be attending the Calgary Olympics in the next two weeks to share the spirit of national unity, and they will be able to hear those announcements in two languages and read the notices in two languages. They will feel at home in a national celebration in both our languages. People will be able to watch it on television in two languages, and be able to feel at home in a western Canadian city because this is a national occasion.
I urge Members of this House not to yield to any hesitation that they may have, to back up the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie), back up the Government, give the Bill a unanimous vote in the House of Commons, and rededicate the spirit of this House to the spirit that we had when we were pioneering in 1969. The unity of the country has been enhanced, the strength of the country has been enhanced, and the spirit and tolerance of our people has been enshrined in the Constitution.
Hear, hear!

I thank the House for the courtesy. I must say that 1 will not argue with the Chair's interpretation of Standing Order 55. I do know that when the Leader of the

Opposition or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) speak in relation to the first reply on a Bill no such courtesy is extended. However, I have been given the courtesy, so I had better put the question.
I was very glad to be here when the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition made his contribution to this Bill. I am also glad that he came to the latter part of his speech, because I have those remarks in his speech of May 20, 1969 as recorded in Hansard on page 8844 when he was the Minister responsible for the introduction of the 1969 Bill.
I do not know if 1 fully appreciated what the Right Hon. Leader said this afternoon in terms of extending the scope of the 1969 Act. When that Bill came in, sold to us, and voted for by me and others following the precept of Bob Stanfield, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, who was then the Minister responsible for the Bill, stated:
The principle of this bill is that there should be equality of access to the
federal institutions of government, that every citizen should be able to
communicate with the federal government in either of the two languages ...
It is not compulsory individual bilingualism; it is institutional bilingualism-
I totally agreed with him there, then, and that was how the Bill was sold, as far as I was concerned.
Today, I understood the Minister to have said that the present Bill C-72 goes further. Perhaps the world has changed. There are bilingual signs at the Olympics, separate and apart from Bill C-72. I think the Right Hon. Leader got carried away with some very interesting remarks that he made. We all know that duality has been extended. There are immersion schools. My children have gone to them, and I have tried to learn la langue J'rangaise-beaucoup de cours de franfais par immersion, et cetera.
We are talking about the reality of Bill C-72. I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman to square with what he said in 1969, and in part what he said today, about the right of institutional bilingualism.
Clause 15(1) states, in effect, that any judge or presiding officer has to carry on without the benefit of an interpreter, that is, be bilingual. That means individual bilingualism. In referring this to Clause 15(2), the definition of court, when 1 make my speech, 1 will give the Right Hon. leader a count of 59 different tribunals or agencies where, until now, an English or French individual can appear quite properly and communicate or correspond, as he or she should be able to. in either language, but the presiding tribunal is not required to be necessarily bilingual. It has simultaneous translation.
Is this not a very real extension of institutional bilingualism, which we all bought and still buy, to a compulsory need for individual bilingualism?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am glad the Hon. Member knew that the time was limited.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member reminds me of the late Syl Apps when he was the captain of the Toronto Maple Leafs. He could never bring the puck up the ice until he had circled the net about four or five times to build up speed.
He was my hero.

I am not saying that the Maple Leafs could not use Syl Apps right now.
The section in the Official Languages Act which the Hon. Member cites has now been embedded in the Constitution, so that the institutional bilingualism he recited is now part of the constitutional fabric of the country.
What has happened in this Bill, as I said, is that it is now enshrining and enacting a practice which has been developed since 1969, recognized by a resolution of the House in 1973, further enshrined in the Constitution Act, 1982, and further enhanced by the Meech Lake Accord. The third paragraph of the preamble to the Bill reads:
AND WHEREAS the Constitution of Canada also provides for guarantees
relating to the right of any member of the public to communicate with, and to
receive available services from, any institution of the Parliament or
Government of Canada in either official language;
Obviously there are not only institutional rights; there are individual rights recognized in this Bill and by the Constitution.

Madam Speaker, I would like to quote the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). He said that the time is right and that the Bill is right. Maybe for the first time the Opposition is right and its leader is right. It is a good Bill.
[ Translation]
I would like to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition on the position he has taken on Bill C-72. I also wish to pay tribute to him and to the other Members of his party who have been working so hard, as was remarked by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), to foster Canada's linguistic duality.
I am also very pleased that you have tried to raise this debate above the level of political partisanship.
The question I would like to ask, and especially the suggestion I would like to make, since all party leaders have their problems-you have yours with Meech Lake, which is also an important piece of constitutional legislation, while other party leaders are trying to convince the majority while maintaining the greatest possible measure of tolerance and respect for the individual.
Mr. Leader of the Opposition, are you and the Members of your party prepared to make a commitment to raise this particular debate above partisan issues during the election campaign, bearing in mind the best interests of Canada's linguistic duality and Canada itself?
February 9, 1988
Madam Speaker, this question is far too important. We do not see it as a partisan issue but as a fundamental question that goes to the very roots of our nation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have just a few minutes remaining, but I want to explain to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) why this Bill is not being accepted by Canadians. It is because of the discriminatory aspect of the Official Languages Act of 1969. I have acted on behalf of many English-speaking Canadians who have been denied promotion and employment because of the discriminatory language laws in this country.
I would like to read to him a case which indicates why western Canadian people are not accepting the Bill. This letter was sent from an official in the Patent Office to a Deputy Minister in Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I worked on this case a couple of years ago. The letter indicates that there were many rumours circulating in the Patent Office that the hiring team, who were then seeking examiners, had been instructed to limit their search to Francophones, particularly to unilingual Francophones. It was further alleged that academically qualified Anglophones had been rejected, and the possibility that these rumours could be true appeared to have been supported by the apparent attempt to keep bilingual positions open for those Francophones being hired rather than offering those positions to bilingual examiners presently in unilingual English positions. Is he telling me that English-speaking Canadians are supposed to accept the Bill when this sort of thing is going on?
This morning I referred to a staff sergeant on the Hill who was demoted because he could not learn French fast enough in that he had a hearing defect. He was demoted. He lost his crown and had a loss of pay. Does the Hon. Member think that I am going to accept that and vote for some more of that? I most certainly am not, and that is what I will be explaining to Canadians.
I have been calling for laws to protect the rights of Englishspeaking Canadians. Former Language Commissioner Maxwell Yalden wanted the word "language" inserted in the Human Rights Act, so that if an academically qualified English-speaking Canadian was being denied promotion or a job, he could file a complaint with the Human Rights Commission to have his case properly investigated to see if he was being treated fairly.
Would the Leader of the Opposition support an amendment to the Human Rights Act to have the word "language" included, so that a Francophone or an Anglophone who is being discriminated against in terms of promotion or employment could file a complaint and have his case properly examined?
Official Languages Act

Madam Speaker, the equality rights of Canadians of either language are protected under the Constitution.
I met recently with Mr. Yalden, the new Human Rights Commissioner, and 1 am assured on his record that he will apply the Constitution and the Human Rights Act fairly in any individual case.
I had the honour, at one stage in my life, of representing a neighbouring riding to that of the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). It happened to be the riding with the largest number of English-speaking public servants in Canada.
I happened to be the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton when I had the honour of presenting the Bill to Parliament. I had the responsibility of explaining it to the Public Service of Canada, of negotiating with C. A. Edwards, the then President of the Public Service Alliance, and of negotiating the terms of the Bill with the four western Attorneys General and persuading them not to take the issue at that time to the Supreme Court of Canada.
I want to say to the hon. gentleman that he has the right and duty to represent his constituents as they present their cases to him, and I respect that. However, I have the feeling in my own experience that this law has been applied as fairly as humanly possible since it was introduced, and that everyone responsible has done his or her best to ensure that the application of the law did not unfairly intervene in a career in the Public Service.
Even after 20 years, as I said earlier in my speech, 60 per cent of designated positions are unilingual English and only 7 per cent are unilingual French. The advantage is still overwhelmingly in favour of the English-speaking population in terms of the Public Service of our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me say that I am pleased to be able to speak today on to the amendments to the Official Languages Act and to talk a little about the official languages policy in the country.
Yesterday and this morning the House was able to hear the views, concerns, obligations, and responsibilities of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) with respect to the courts under the current Act and indeed to some of the proposed changes in the Act. We also heard this morning from the Minister of State (Mr. Lewis) regarding language rights and opportunities in respect of services in federal institutions.
My particular role as Secretary of State is somewhat different and has perhaps not received the same kind of attention as have other interested perspectives in respect of this Bill. Clauses 40 to 44 deal with those responsibilities which are given to the Secretary of State. They amount to two. First, there is the responsibility to recognize the use and learning of both official languages. Second, support is to be provided to official language communities across the country.

February 9, 1988
Official Languages Act
Those two responsibilities given to the Secretary of State under this Bill reflect what we have been doing for the last 18 years. It extends what we have been doing somewhat, but there has been a slow progression of events. It fits in well with the role of the Secretary of State because the Secretary of State has a general responsibility with respect to the sense of belonging and equal participation of all Canadians from all walks of life. That is why it is important that at least a significant part of this Bill be understood within the context of other initiatives that the Government, and in particular the Secretary of State, have been taking with respect to, for example, the new multicultural Bill and the amendments to the Citizenship Act. In all these matters, whether it is the multicultural Bill, changes to the Official Languages Act or changes to the Citizenship Act, we are responding as a Government to three fundamental principles that the Government, and I think all Canadian Governments at their best, stand for. That is to say equality, diversity and community.
Those may be cliches and principles unrelated to practice to some people. However, when we talk about those principles and try to deal with them in legislation we are on very serious business. When we talk in this instance about language and culture we only have to watch television, read newspapers and look around the world to see those countries which have not paid attention to the divisiveness of language and culture. In those countries their problems have been solved by conflict and not by co-operation and consensus.
When we deal with the Bill before us, with the multicultural Bill and our understanding of the Citizenship Act amendments we are responding to the principles of equality, diversity and community. It should never be forgotten that the end result is freedom for individual Canadians and stability for Canadian society as a whole.
[ Translation]
Madam Speaker, our official languages are a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society. They set us apart from most nations in this world.
This linguistic duality gives all Canadian citizens the right to live and develop their potential in either official language.
Madam Speaker, language is a very personal part of ourselves. If we can all learn to respect the language spoken by our fellow citizens, we will have made an important contribution to tolerance and harmony among the various races, creeds and cultures that constitute our country.

We have been in the business of dealing with two official languages for a very long time. It is not merely and only a product of 1969. Earlier, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) talked about the constitutional and legal process which over decades was dealt with in our two official languages. We could go back even further. We could begin in 1867. At another time and another place it would be
interesting to note that there is a 200-year old tradition in the country from the Quebec Act of 1774 to the Constitution Act of 1791 to the British North America Act of 1867. We have been involved in developing, building, creating, fashioning and tolerating two languages for 200 years.
With respect to specific changes in the role of federal institutions as they relate to the two official languages, I think we can mark the beginning of the modern era, if I can put it that way, in 1934 when the Secretary of State, under the prime ministership of R. B. Bennett, introduced into the House a Bill that created a translation service for the federal Government. That was some 54 years ago. In a sense, that was the first practical example of the need to ensure that federal institutions spoke to all Canadians in both official languages.
In 1958, for the first time in the history of the country, a Translation service was brought into the Flouse. We are used to it today. We simply put a small device into our ears and we are able to listen to an automatic, first-class translation of the proceedings. That began only in 1958, I might add, with some price, under the prime ministership of John George Diefen-baker.
In 1969, when the Official Languages Act was adopted, it should not be forgotten that all three political Parties supported that Bill and have done so since that time.
1 have gone through these events because it is important to understand that history did not begin yesterday. These important matters did not begin when we showed up. They have been part of the Canadian understanding of our country as long as we have been around. It is fair to say that since the 1960s the climate with respect to the language question has improved immeasurably.
For the past 20 years we have seen an emerging positive and impressive growth of the use of those two languages. That may be denied by some. But all one has to do is to attend meetings anywhere in the country where people from other parts of the country are brought in. One will find that there is some facility so that people in both languages can understand.
If I had to pick one example to illustrate my points I would like to introduce some statistics, although I hate to use them, with respect to the success enjoyed by immersion courses in schools, institutions and community groups across the country. For the past 10 years enrolment in terms of immersion courses has increased 20 per cent per year. It has grown from 37,000 in 1977 to over 200,000 in 1987. In Alberta, one out of every ten schools is a French immersion school. In Regina, the number of students enrolled in French immersion courses was 60 in 1977. It was 3,000 in 1987.
How about Toronto and Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My friend the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition asks about Toronto and Vancouver. There has been amazing growth in those cities as well. I picked these other
February 9, 1988

cities to illustrate my point. In every province and in every major metropolitan area, city and town one will find such statistics. My right hon. friend knows that, as do the great majority of Canadians, certainly those who are interested in these matters.
In fact, there was a study done by Stacy Churchill and Anthony Smith which showed a major shift in Canadian attitudes towards language reform, use and the recognition of the two official languages. That is shown by incredible demands on my own Department with respect to supporting the provision of minority language services. I suppose that if one had to see it anywhere one would see it in the habits and instincts of young Canadians. Their feeling for the linguistic duality of this country is something that previous generations would not have dreamed of.
It is these young Canadians who are learning a second official language who hold a big promise for us. I have had the opportunity in meetings across the country with young people to see that not only do they understand the importance of language for their own community but they understand the importance of extending that to the other official language groups as well. I think that they see the benefit of being able to speak two languages in a world whose borders are coming closer and where travel, politics, education and international trade will welcome those who are able to avail themselves of a natural resource, that is, of the two official languages. I might add, as I have in other places and at other times, that a multitude of heritage languages also exist in Canada.
The Bill as it relates to the Ministry of the Secretary of State is very important. It deals with the encouragement, the recognition, the use and the learning of two official languages. It also deals with the support of official language communities. We do that in deliberate, constructive ways. For example, through agreements since 1980 with provinces and territories, we support educational programs and services for Englishspeaking Quebecers and for Francophones outside the Province of Quebec.
We provide opportunities for all Canadians to learn a second language. The summer language bursary program is particularly popular. It gives students the chance to spend six weeks immersed in their second language. Over 19,000 students applied for 7,250 bursaries last year.
We also support the development of teacher-training programs in universities and colleges across Canada, from Memorial University to all three universities in the Province of British Columbia. As well, the Government assists provinces and territories in developing learning materials. Our commitment to the development of TV Ontario's La Chaine Frangaise is an example of this.
TV Ontario now offers Franco-Ontarians the same kind of educational programming English-speaking students have had for years. It has also developed, with federal assistance, a
Official Languages Act
number of excellent programs on TV Ontario to teach French as a second language.
In short, this Bill stresses the importance of giving Canadians the opportunity to expand their horizons by learning a second language. The Bill responds to the linguistic needs and aspirations of Canadians, make no mistake about that. It is for Canadians who want for themselves and their children the opportunity to be themselves in their own language wherever they live in Canada, Canadians who want for themselves and their children the opportunity to learn a second official language and Canadians who realize that having two official languages gives us access to over half the people on this planet. That puts us in a first-class strategic position in terms of trade advantages, international relations and cultural exchanges.
The Government's approach is a positive one. It is based on incentives, consultations and partnership. Jean Pelletier of the Journal de Montreal, wrote about Bill C-72 a few weeks ago. He said:
Some of the most striking changes are reflected in the preamble of the
Bill... It removes the Act from the realm of mere rules and regulations and
elevates it to the status of a law that-can serve as an inspiration for the dayto-day political life of this country.

The time has come to offer Canadians throughout this country a better chance to develop their potential in their own official language.

I had the opportunity, as all Secretaries of State do, to visit with people across the country, not only with constituents and people I am trying to serve but with members of official language communities, both francophone and anglophone. It was a very impressive opportunity and I wish all Canadians could have that opportunity.

The Government directly helps minority communities to acquire tools and establish institutions, which enables these communities to participate in various aspects of Canadian society in their own language.
We support a number of groups representing Francophone communities across Canada, such as the Federation des francophones hors Quebec, the Association canadienne-franpaise de l'Ontario, French-speaking Canadians in British Columbia, Newfoundland and the Northwest Territories, and many other groups I had a chance to meet last year in Winnipeg, Yellowknife and Charlottetown, for instance.
These groups provide for solidarity and community action. They make it possible for communities to express their views and carry out collective projects.
Francophones in Halifax-Dartmouth or in Cape St. George, Newfoundland can get together and set up a community and education centre, jointly financed by the federal-provincial governments.

February 9, 1988
Official Languages Act
The Federation des jeunes canadiens-fran^ais is organizing a project for community radio across the country. Programming will be developed by the communities themselves. And the Department of the Secretary of State is of course proud to support this project!

I also had the opportunity to meet a group of which 1 did not have much knowledge before. This group consists of small anglophone communities in the Province of Quebec, outside the Island of Montreal. There is, I think, an unintended feeling in other parts of the country that Anglophones live in Montreal only and that, by and large that is whom we hear about.
I had the terrific opportunity to meet with members of an Alliance Quebec as well as regional grassroots organizations including the Committee for Anglophone Social Action of the Gaspe, the Townshippers' Association of the Eastern Townships, the Outaouais Alliance of the Ottawa Valley, the Voice of English Quebec of the Quebec City area and many others. They introduced me, as they would introduce all of us, to a very impressive piece of Canadian history. They have a network of 14 weekly newspapers, some of which have been around, informing, building and helping create communities, for decades.
The Stanstead Journal in Rock Island has existed since 1845. The West Quebec Post in Buckingham has been there since 1895. The Watchman in Lachute has been there since 1877. My impression of these communities is that not only were they appreciating their own history but they knew that they were building their own communities as Quebecers and as Canadians. That impressed me. The reason I mention it in this context is that they support this Bill. They do so because they know that the programs we have been offering and want to continue to offer and expand support those anglophone communities in the Province of Quebec.
I also had the opportunity to deal with another group, nongovernmental. There are a great many voluntary organizations and business organizations which are now and have been for the last couple of years interested in getting support to expand opportunities in Canada's two official languages. Mr. Lloyd McGinnis, past chairman of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, has said:
Modern business managers in Canada-recognize that it makes good
business sense to employ communications tools that capitalize on both official
languages.
That is why, on a voluntary basis, the Secretary of State has received requests from bodies and organizations wanting to serve clients in English and in French. Two examples of this are the Canadian Bankers Association and the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association. My Department assists 275 voluntary groups in bilingual services at conferences and annual meetings, and more than 60 major associations are being helped with bilingualism development plans.
We support organizations such as Canadian Parents for French. One of the most impressive groups we support is the
Canadian Society of Association Executives with well over 1,200 member associations. On their own initiative, its representatives came to see me in order to establish a program of assistance for private and voluntary groups promoting both official languages. I say these things because that is the reality in Canada and we ought to begin to understand it.
1 know that my time has concluded. I would like to finish with one final remark. The Government is committed not only to strengthening the official languages in Canada, it also understands that in doing so, there is something greater at stake and that is the fundamental proposition, that we must continue to support the development of the community of Canada. We can only do that when we rise to the challenge and recognize that being Canadian means we should continue the tradition of two official languages and move forward.
I hope the House will be able to conclude the debate and we can get it into committee to deal with those matters which are of concern to some people. However, at the end of the day we will have failed the promise of this country if we do not move forward, as the Government would like to with changes to the Official Languages Act that tell Canadians and the world that we have not forgotten the great traditions of this country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments.

Madam Speaker, being also a Member from Ontario as the Minister is, I would like to commend him, first for his speech and second for that part of his speech he chose to deliver in French in this House this afternoon. I suggest this reflects an open mind, and that special effort by the Minister deserves to be emphasized today.
Especially since he is a former mayor of Toronto!

Yes, especially from a former mayor of Toronto, Madam Speaker!
1 pay close attention to the Minister's comments. I may have a slightly different opinion from his in that he is hoping for an early conclusion to the debate, and 1 would welcome an opportunity to make a speech in this House on this matter. I represent in this Parliament the largest number of Francophones outside Quebec of any constituency, and this is why 1 am hoping for such an opportunity. Needless to say, 1 am hoping contrary to the Minister that the debate will last at least one or two more days, so that I also can take part in it and express my support for the Official Languages Bill.
1 suggest, Madam Speaker, that in view of the official languages situation at this stage in Canada, it is important to have Bill C-72, even though the legislation holds nothing new; by that I mean that we need Bill C-72 because we need a vehicle to re-emphasize our commitment to official languages,
February 9, 1988

and of course there are many more reasons why we want Bill C-72. Flon. Members explained them and I also will discuss them when I rise in this debate.
I simply wish to put a specific question to the Minister concerning the Supreme Court. As far as I am concerned, I feel that the clause providing that the presiding member of a panel of judges hearing a party to the proceedings must be able to do so in that party's language. There is one exemption to that rule under the Bill, being the Supreme Court of Canada. I have no idea, Madam Speaker, why they chose to do that. I would like to ask the Minister whether in committee the Government would accept to change that, even if it entails extending the period for the Supreme Court to adapt to that new recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first let me assure the Hon. Member that, as always, we listen to his remarks with interest and we are sure he has some wisdom to offer to the House. When I indicated that 1 hoped the debate would be concluded,
I of course meant after all Hon. Members had the opportunity to make their contribution.
The second part of the Hon. Member's question dealt with changes to the Bill which he favours. When the Minister of Justice spoke the other day, I think it is fair to say that he indicated that there needs to be a capacity in each of our courts, and I think the emphasis should be on the word "capacity", and that it excludes the Supreme Court. I think the Minister dealt with that, I am not sure. It may well be that there are other views. I am sure that when it gets into committee any specific changes that Hon. Members are looking for will at least be appropriately considered by the committee.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the Minister concerning the situation of the Anglophone in Quebec. Having lived there for a while, I saw what happened when Bill 101 was brought into force and the effect it had on anglophone Quebecers most of the young Anglophones had to leave the province because they were being discriminated against. Therefore, would the Minister consider a motion of the House asking the Government of Quebec to withdraw Bill 101, as was done in the case of Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should remind the Hon. Member that Bill 101 is a provincial Bill and at least some aspects of it are before the courts. It would therefore be inappropriate for me to deal with that aspect of it.
However, let me respond to what I think might be the spirit of the question, which is something that I tried to deal with in my own speech. Clauses 40 to 44 are positive ways where we do not try to recapture the past but try to see what we can do to fashion a future. It is always an easy way out for people to bog down because of their understanding of things in the past. I appreciate that because I have been involved with it myself in a number of circumstances. However, in our circumstances today, I hope what Hon. Members will do is to look at the
Official Languages Act
positive things in Bill C-72 that deal with Anglophones in the Province of Quebec, and there are many of them. I have met with those people and their organizations, such as the ones I mentioned in the Gaspe, the Outaouais, in the Comtes de I'Est. They want to be part of a society that respects their heritage, understands them as Quebecers and as Canadians. That is what this Bill does and I commend that to my hon. friend.

Madam Speaker, we all concur with the Minister's comments dealing with voluntary French immersion in our schools. In Peterborough we have a line-up to enrol in those schools, and 1 think the voluntary approach is a good one. 1 think it is also a good approach for the private sector which has indicated its interest in obtaining information and advancing this voluntarily in the private sector. The aspects of this Bill which are a little repugnant are those that change from the voluntary to the mandatory.
1 would like to ask the Minister at what point it is the Government's intention to cause a region to become bilingual, thus falling under-the Minister has a question mark in his eyes. We have a language of work in approximately seven regions of this country as defined in our legislation and in the understanding of the Department of Justice. There is the rest of Canada to deal with. This Bill makes it possible, through regulations and Orders in Council, to declare regions bilingual. At what point does a region become bilingual by Order in Council, thus causing this Bill to take effect through mandatory regulations enforced by Orders in Council? We as backbenchers have no idea at what point or with what regulations that will happen.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member understands, as I do, that regulations are important, particularly with respect to a Bill of this nature. It is the regulations that take the words in the Bill and turn them into practical day-to-day living. I was very pleased therefore to hear the Minister of Justice indicate that when the regulations are brought down there will be an opportunity for full public exposure and debate. At that time I am sure the Hon. Member's question will be answered.

Madam Speaker, the Minister referred to the fact that certain segments of Bill 101 in Quebec are before the courts. Would the Minister comment on the timing of this Bill? One of the things that is probably of concern to some Members is why the federal Government would bring forward Bill C-72 when we have still not been able to resolve the problems and attitudes expressed in Bill 101.
While he is on his feet would the Minister also try to define "significant demand"?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, "significant demand" will be defined by regulation. As I indicated in response to the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm), when the

February 9, 1988
Adjournment Debate
regulations come down, significant demand in a particular area will be understood in the full glare of public exposure and public discussion. 1 commend that process to the Hon. Member because I think that is the fair and open way to do it.
With regard to the impact of Bill 101 in the Province of Quebec, as I indicated earlier there are aspects, in particular signage, before the courts and I would not want to comment on them. I would, however, say again to this Hon. Member that anglophone communities in the Province of Quebec support this Bill. People can play around with that fact all they like, but the reality is that if one is interested in supporting not only francophone communities across the country but anglophone communities in Quebec, one should do one's duty and support this Bill.

speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 66, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway)- Interprovincial trade-Removal of barriers; the Hon.
