The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to join in a very important debate on Bill C-72 which amends and re-enacts the Official Languages Act of 1969. I am honoured to follow the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) who both joined in the debate this afternoon.
When this Bill was originally tabled in the House I had expected that I would be the first speaker on it from our
caucus. However, when the debate was scheduled for Monday of this week I found myself in one of those conflicts which Members of Parliament have occasionally. I had a commitment to travel 250 kilometers north of Thunder Bay to the small community of Armstrong in order to present some Celebration '88 medals and scrolls to people in that community. I did not think it was fair to them to ask for a drastic rearrangement of timetables in order to allow me to come here.
I am grateful to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar), for the able way in which she addressed the topic before us yesterday morning. She spoke skilfully from her experience here in the national capital area on the importance of official languages and put it in a variety of contexts which are important to Canadians.
Today 1 want to take up something of the attitudes which have been expressed here in the House and outside the House and to elaborate on the support which 1 think exists in Canada for Bill C-72 for a strengthening of the laws dealing with official bilingualism in this country. I do this all the more because of the report in The Globe and Mail specifically which suggested that the Ministers speaking yesterday in support of Bill C-72 were being heckled by back-benchers in their own caucus, a highly unusual situation and one which certainly arouses one's interest.
1 have asked my colleagues about the strength of this opposition, if you will, in the Conservative caucus to Bill C-72.
1 gather that "heckled" may be over-doing it a little bit, although the questions being posed this afternoon to the Secretary of State suggest the concerns which a variety of back-bench Members feel.
I was distressed earlier today when listening to the Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) on this topic to sense much more than only concern about the way in which the Official Languages Act might impact on individuals in various ways. I was particularly distressed to hear him taking statistics on the advance of bilingualism in various areas of the federal Government as evidence of a dangerous tendency, or at least that is what I inferred from it. He appeared to suggest that these advances in bilingual ability to some very high and impressive proportions in certain areas of the federal Government were a bad thing.
I suspect that what he was thinking in the first order, and trying to suggest to all of us here and those outside listening to the debate, was that these bilingual persons were persons whose first language was French and that these proportions suggested an overwhelming employment in these various areas of government of persons who were francophones as against anglophones in the Canadian population. That would certainly be a concern given the principle of equitable participation if employment in various areas of government ran to three-quarters and more of francophone Canadians. I could understand concern among Anglophones across the country because employment in the Public Service is a desirable form of service
February 9, 1988

to the country and persons whose first language is English want to share in that opportunity to serve.
I think, however, that he failed to recognize the fact that many of the persons who are included in these statistics are persons whose first language is English, who have become bilingual and who, by being bilingual, enhance the service they can give the people of Canada and enhance the abilities of the Public Service to operate in both languages.
In pursuing that I want to make something of a report in Language and Society published by the Office of the Commissioner of Official Languages in April, 1987. There is an article in here by Stacy Churchill and Anthony Smith to which I believe the Secretary of State referred. I would like to pull some sections of this particular article from it for all of us to contemplate because I think that few of us appreciate that attitudes in the country have been changing since the Official Languages Act in 1969 responded to a political challenge, in Quebec particularly but out of Quebec as well. In that response the Official Languages Act has loosed a ferment, if you will, in the Canadian population which has been modifying the culture of the country in ways which I personally regard as desirable.
These two sociologists first consider the ways in which attitudes across the country are sensitive to the bilingual reality, to English and French. They put Quebec beside British Columbia assuming that these might be our polar opposites, one society being first French-speaking and the other being largely English-speaking. They note that an astounding 99 per cent of Quebecers consider the ability to speak both English and French to be very or moderately important in helping a young person get ahead. Fully 93 per cent of Quebecers believe that English and French should be required in school. They note that Quebecers are almost as supportive of the language rights of the English-speaking minority as they are positive about the value of learning English. Eighty-eight per cent of Quebec's Francophones believe that Anglophones in Quebec should be entitled to education for their children in English. Eighty-nine per cent believe that English-speaking residents of Quebec should be able to receive hospital service in English. Support for service in English in the Post Office is 85 per cent and in department stores 82 per cent.
Those are impressive figures in a province in which Conservative back-benchers have been obsessed about Bill 101 as reflecting a reality in Quebec.
What are the attitudes in British Columbia as far as acceptance of English and French in various ways is concerned? This public opinion poll is a Canadian fact survey which the Commissioner of Official Languages commissioned in 1985. It indicates that 69 per cent of the British Columbia population believe that speaking both English and French is important to a young person getting ahead. Seventy-seven per cent think it would be beneficial if all Canadians spoke both
Official Languages Act
English and French, and 59 per cent support the compulsory teaching of both languages in schools. This is in a province where the francophone population in 1981 was not even 2 per cent. Fifty-seven per cent of the population in British Columbia believe that people who live in the province and speak French should be entitled to education for their children in French. Similarly, a majority of 55 per cent of British Columbians believe that hospital services should be available to Francophones in French.
As the authors suggest, what is desirable in exploring this matter of service of official bilingualism is to put it in a human context in terms of services to real people. There is not the kind of fear that Western Report is pandering to or the kind of prejudice that still exists in some minds, but the kind of compassion that I believe characterizes Canadians as they recognize that official bilingualism is a humane response to part of the reality of the Canadian population.
The authors conclude that the national picture is a positive one over-all. The levels of support for service in the language of the provincial minorities is at the 50 per cent level or better on all questions asked, including those which deal with both the public sector and the private sector.
For those outside Quebec, the support is 50 per cent or better on all questions asked about the public sector. What I find quite astonishing is that outside Quebec 40 per cent or more of the Canadian population believe that institutions in the private sector should be prepared to serve Canadians in both official languages. Such an astonishing change in attitude of Canadians leaves no doubt that in the last 20 years a cultural revolution has been under way. Bill C-72 is designed to support and enhance that change in attitude among most Canadians.
The authors recognize that a minority in this poll feel differently. If we want to use the public opinion poll data to create a profile of Canadians least likely to support bilingualism, it would single out an Anglophone, 50 years of age or over, with no past training in French as a second language, no current contact with the French language, living in western Canada. I hesitate over those last words. I am western Canadian myself in origin and I think it is important to recognize that there is this minority feeling across the country, including various parts of Ontario and Atlantic Canada. It is clearly a minority, but one that is decreasing.
Canadians of all ages believe that bilingualism is a useful skill for young people, even if older Canadians do not consider bilingualism valuable for themselves personally. That in itself is evidence of how this country is changing and developing.
Bill C-72 allows us to explore ways in which the Official Languages Act of 1969, which was supported by all Parties in Parliament and enhanced by the Charter in 1982, can be strengthened. This includes explicitly addressing the question of cost in accomplishing this goal. Undoubtedly there is a cost attached, but we should be capable of recognizing that governments make decisions that cost money. The argument

February 9, 1988
Official Languages Act
that an expenditure must be carried out is not valid because countries spend money in various ways to enhance the unity and strength of a nation. In terrible circumstances, countries are forced to make expenditures to suppress minorities or maintain forces of occupation.
Rather than being forced to make expenditures in such ugly circumstances, we spend money on the cultivation of both languages, to encourage immersion programs across the country, which have been spectacularly successful. Government expenditures are used to support organizations such as Canadian Parents for French, a group which reflects the change that has taken place in this country.
I suggest that the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars each year in these areas is a good investment, and one that we should continue to make.
Therefore, speaking for my colleagues in the New Democratic Party caucus:

-we remain committed to the cause of generally promoting the official languages in Canadian society, co-operation with the provinces in that respect, particularly assistance to official languages minorities, and the opportunity for all to learn the second official language.

That is the position that the New Democratic Party has taken over the years, and it is one in which we are solid today. We supported the goals of the Official Languages Act of 1969 and we recognize that, considering the developing circumstances in the country today, it is advisable to have an amendment and re-enactment of the Act. We support Bill C-72 in its attempt to address the desire of Canadians to work in the Public Service in the language of their choice as well as to deal with the Government in the language with which they are most familiar and best able to express themselves.
At the press conference following the tabling of the Bill last June there was a very warm pouring out of support for the Bill from various quarters, to which I joined to some extent. There may have been some satisfaction as well as pleasure about the fact that the Conservative Government, which we realize includes Members who are concerned about what official bilingualism represents, was able to introduce a Bill with as good and varied provisions as Bill C-72 has. When I saw it against the current of approbation for the Bill, to express a concern or two, I did not get anywhere with the media, as anyone can see simply by going back and looking at the coverage in the Ottawa Citizen and other newspapers.
Without diminishing any of that support this afternoon, I would like to express those same concerns here and add one or two others. My concern at the time focused primarily on the statements dealing with service in Clause 31 of the Bill and with equitable participation, as the jargon goes, and with the
matter of fairness of employment, if you will, with which Clause 38 deals.
Clause 31(2) provides for the prescribing of circumstances in which there is a significant demand for the purpose of service to the public. This is by no means a simple matter. My concern is primarily that the situation previously was one in which the obligation was on Government to provide service to the official language minority except where the demand was so low or uneven as to be unjustified. As a member of the Standing Joint Committee on Official Languages, I can tell my colleagues in the House that government action under this section, that is, service to the public by Departments and agencies and Crown corporations, has been advanced only very, very slowly over the years. It is astonishing that in the mid-1980s one still has to bludgeon various Crown corporations, in particular, and to a lesser extent Departments of the Government, to achieve this matter of service to the public.
This is simple humanity. If someone who is unilingual French or who is far more fluent in French than in English approaches Government, it is only simple humanity that the government Department or Crown corporation be prepared to serve him or her in that language. The fact that it has taken so long is quite a commentary on the fact that the Act of 1969 laid on the obligation except where demand was low or uneven.
I put that as the background against which we have now, in a sense, a change in posture. Government will specify what the requirements of significant demand are and the public will have the opportunity to bring legal pressure to bear. It is certainly the tradition to use litigation these days to advance the cause, and official language minorities certainly know a great deal about being forced to use litigation. Frankly, 1 am not at all happy about the possibility that people are going to have to use litigation. That route will be used because of a political failure of the will of Government. That is one of the parts which concerns me.
With respect to Clause 38, the provision is for a Public Service which will tend to reflect the Canadian population that may do the job, although this will even more clearly require will on the part of the Government of the day. The phrase "tend to reflect" is really pretty loose. I would like to see much stronger language, although I would say this is very much in keeping with Bill C-62, the employment equity Bill, which was all too weak as well. I am not all that surprised to have this sort of legislation from this Conservative Government.
These are concerns which I articulated last June and I appreciate the opportunity today to state them again. There are other concerns which I will not have the time to address with respect to the main comments expressed by the Governments of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Those are points that certainly will be put forward at committee. I believe my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin), will certainly want to expand on those points at an early point in the debate. I am sorry I will not have the time
February 9, 1988

myself, unless someone places a question and I can say something about it.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member noted his concurrence with Part VI, participation of English speaking and French speaking Canadians, and employment opportunities. The intent of the Bill is, of course, to give equal opportunity to both English and French to participate in this program, according to this Bill. I wonder if the Hon. Member could explain how we can have equal participation in the Bill when the Bill specifically states that it is a requirement, once an area is designated bilingual, that any supervisory or management functions which are to be carried out by those institutions are to be done in both official languages? That is according to Clause 37(l)(a)(iii). I wonder if he would explain how that is going to happen if the person is unilingual.

Mr. Speaker, 1
appreciate the question. The matter of equitable participation does not establish a general right for any and all Anglophones to serve in government. I was reminded of a struggle for a Supreme Court position in the United States some years ago. I believe it was a Senator from North Dakota who argued that mediocrity had a right to a place on the Supreme Court of the United States. Simply because he had been described as mediocre was no reason why he should not be appointed to the position.
That incident comes to mind because what we are clearly approaching is the development of a Public Service in Canada which has some new characteristics. It is a Public Service which, at its higher levels, in particular, will be bilingual. It will be a Public Service, the supervisors of which will be capable of dealing with their subordinates in English or in French, depending on which language their subordinates would like to work in. That, I recognize, creates pinches along the way. It creates the challenge to learn the other language, a challenge which faces so many persons in public life.
On the way to doing that, there will be people who think it is all terribly unfair and that it is not a matter of equality. But equitable participation is primarily a matter of ensuring that there is opportunity for minorities, the English language minority in Quebec and the French speaking minority across the country. We want to be sure that as the Public Service develops over time, we move closer to having a reflection of the Canadian population in Government. That is clearly the direction in which public opinion expects Government to move. French immersion classes outside of Quebec are so spectacularly successful these days because parents recognize they need to prepare their children for a time when the Canadian elite, if you will, will be bilingual. That elite in the Public Service of Canada will be capable of working in either language.

Madam Speaker, may I say through you to the member of the Opposition, that I fail to see the logic of the Hon. Member's statement that it is fair to Anglophones in Quebec, as the Hon. Member has mentioned, in supplying this position of supervisory or management function, because the
Official Languages Act
unilingual Anglophone in Quebec would have no chance under this legislation, according to Clause 37(l)(a)(iii) which simply states that any supervisory or management functions that are to be carried out in both official languages by that management team.
How does the Hon. Member propose to protect unilingual Anglophones or unilingual Francophones with this legislation in the workplace? How can they improve their position by advancement through management to top positions if they are unilingual? I fail to see the fairness.

Madam Speaker, if the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) would look at Clause 37, he would note that subclause (1) states:
The Treasury Board may make regulations in respect of federal
institutions,-
The Bill goes on to set forth the goals of our policy. The "may make" is clearly an indication that there will be recognition of rights. Grandfathering has gone on throughout the Public Service for a long time in a straightforward manner, often to the detriment of the policy that was expressed in the Bill of 1969.
I am sure that tender regard for the rights of individuals, and their assertions through one organization or another, will provide protection as we move toward the goal that the majority of Canadians want, whether or not the Hon. Member for Simcoe South thinks that this is all terribly funny. He is in the minority. The minority or the silent majority, as they would like to think of themselves, are the silent majority of the 19th century, those dead and gone.

The Hon. Member is misinterpreting the legislation before us. When the Hon. Member quotes Clause 37(1), "The Treasury Board may make regulations", we are talking about making regulations deeming such things as that other areas in respect of Canada or places outside of Canada shall become bilingual by designation.
There are seven areas in Canada which are now deemed to be bilingual in the workplace, and let us deal with those seven. How does one protect a unilingual Anglophone in the Province of Quebec who wants to be in mid-management when it is a prerequisite under this Bill that that management position be filled with a bilingual person?
While the Hon. Member is answering that question, will he tell me how to protect a Francophone in the rest of Canada who cannot speak fluently class C or a top grade of English, in order that he can advance through the Public Service in Alberta when he is not fluently bilingual? He cannot take a management position, according to this Bill that we are studying today, and the clause referred to by the Hon. Member, with all due respect, does not deal with a designated bilingual place or region in the workplace.

February 9, 1988
Official Languages Act

There are two realities here. One is the practice for years past in which many odd things go on for the protection of those who are unilingual. All sorts of odd things have gone on, and I expect all sorts of odd things will go on in the future for the protection of those persons.
Early in 1988, 19 years after the Official Languages Act became law, and long after the anglophone population of Quebec should have faced up to reality, and I assume the Hon. Member is talking about an Anglophone Quebecer, if the Hon. Member asks me how I am going to protect such a person, I am not sure how much I want to do to protect such a person.
Right.

A person living in Quebec who is still unilingual after all those years with all the assistance that the federal Government can provide in the way of language study, knowing full well that that is what advancement in the Public Service requires, and knowing this reality for the past two decades, how far does one extend the compassion that the Canadian population generally feels, which I was invoking earlier, when one is on the brink of testing that compassion?
There are challenges to be met. Anglophone Canadians can meet that challenge in the same way as Francophone Canadians. I am sure that all of us have watched with some interest the manner in which the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), who came out of the francophone context, has learned English and how to operate in the House. He deserves a lot of credit for doing that.
Personally, 1 do not think that George Bain's observation some 20 years ago, and I remember the column well in The Globe and Mail about this strange malady suffered by western Canadians, the inability to learn French, is anything but a satirical observation by a commentator who knew which way things were moving in this country, and had to.

Madam Speaker, I have barely four minutes left but I will undoubtedly have other opportunities to pursue the debate.
From the outset I should like to say that Bill C-72 is one of the major components of the over-all proposition made by this Government in terms of unity and national reconciliation. Since the Meech Lake Accord did acknowledge the existence
of two linguistic communities in this country, it is important to point out the federal Government's commitment not only to acknowledge this linguistic duality but also to promote it throughout Canada.
Briefly now, some of my colleagues seem to be concerned about the difficulties this Bill might create for their fellow citizens.
There is talk of possible discrimination in employment, and some of my colleagues rapidly produced protest letters referring to language discrimination. 1 want to tell my colleagues that for every such letter they have I can produce 1,000. Yes, 1,000 letters about discrimination-alleged or otherwise-against the Canadian francophone minority. One has to be wary of such literature and such statements. It is a ready-made excuse, such an easy way to hide one's lack of experience and qualifications: I was not selected or I was not promoted because I speak French or because 1 speak English. What an easy way out! One has to be careful. I have had people coming up to me and say: I did not get the job because I am Francophone. A check into the matter showed that such was not the case, the person involved simply did not have the qualifications required for senior management.
On this point, the clause of Bill C-72 is very clear:

Clause 38(3) reads:
Merit principle (3) Nothing in this section shall be construed as abrogating
or derogating from the principle of selection of personnel according to merit.

This section, therefore, will not change anything to the mode of selection based on the merit principle. And that remains a basic criterion.
Madam Speaker, some of my colleagues often refer to Bill 101. Strangely enough, they are representatives from other provinces. The main reason Quebec felt compelled to adopt Bill 101, is because this country, in the past, would not respect the Canadian linguistic duality and had failed to show enough generosity to make us feel fully at home in Canada.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   PUBLIC EMPLOYEES POLITICAL RIGHTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-273, an Act respecting political rights of public servants, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise today, as the only public servant who was elected in the last federal general election, to speak on my Bill C-273 designed to extend political rights to public servants. I have spoken on this issue on a number of occasions in the past, the first time being my maiden speech in this place in November, 1984. It gives me some pleasure now to present legislation aimed at redressing what I view as an injustice. I believe firmly that this is an issue which should transcend Party affiliation. It is an area that all Parties and Members have an interest in promoting, and it can demonstrate how well the House can work when an issue that all Canadians see as important is brought before it.
I should like to highlight briefly why I feel that the issue is an important one. The report on equality rights presented to Parliament in 1985 noted the following:
While the neutrality of the Public Service must be preserved as a general
principle, it seems to us that the rights of public servants are, at least in certain
circumstances, unduly curtailed.
In my view that is a classic understatement.
There is a fundamental issue at stake here-whether a group of Canadians has the right to free speech, free assembly, and the right to work peacefully and lawfully for democratic change. Hundreds, perhaps thousands, of public servants all across Canada who have participated in the election campaigns of all three Parties have had to look over their shoulders, worrying that big brother working out of the Public Service Commission office would discipline them for stuffing envelopes or painting lawn signs. Drivers, clerks, or technical staff whose work may never touch upon policy cannot join their neighbours in the simplest of election tasks without risk of losing their jobs.
Balanced against the claim that basic rights are being denied is the argument that political activity would jeopardize the neutrality of the Public Service and undermine the effective administration of government policy.
The debate over the political rights of public servants must take into account that the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees everyone in Canada freedom of conscience, thought, belief, opinion, and expression. The Charter clearly states that these rights are subject only to such "reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society".
Public Employees Political Rights
Therefore, two obligations exist in this debate. Those of us who defend the right of public servants to political expression must answer legitimate questions raised about the effects of such expression on the effective administration of public policy. Those who would deprive public servants of their democratic rights must show that the limitations are "demonstrably justified".
The objections to allowing public servants the opportunity to enjoy democratic rights are not superficial. Indeed, they go to the core of our beliefs of how a democratic government should function. These objections are rooted in the idea that the expression of Party loyalty or political orientation by public servants would endanger the public perception of neutrality, allow public servants to promote their personal political philosophies in advice to Ministers, and put Party interest above service to the public in the implementation of policy.
However, are we to assume that the only people who have a political philosophy are those who are active members of a political Party? Moreover, just as we are aware that there are active members of political Parties who have no discernible political philosophy aside from self-interest, we know of how profoundly the political philosophies of supposedly neutral public servants have affected the development of public policy in the country.
The fact is that whether or not public servants belong to a political Party or stuff envelopes in an election campaign, their political philosophies will remain intact. Preventing them from speaking or from participating in the political process will not stop them from thinking.
This is not to deny the rights to which both Ministers and the public are entitled in their expectations of service from the bureaucracy. However, neither the public nor cabinet Ministers have the right to the illusion that public servants have no political opinions. Rather, they have a right to have those opinions expressed visibly, so that some sort of accountability may be carried out. There is no protection for the public with a muzzled Public Service, only an increased opportunity for the obtrusive influence of personal and hidden views.
With the open declaration of political affiliation, any public servant with a partisan affiliation will be constrained to behave in an objective manner when dealing with both the public and his or her colleagues, to demonstrate that political bias does not exist.
Nothing in the restoration of political rights to public servants through the Bill removes the burden on the Public Service of behaving in a non-partisan manner in the execution of public duties. There is, of course, nothing unethical in the expression of political opinion. The essential question is whether public servants will act to implement government policy in a non-partisan manner, not whether they have personal views on politics or a political philosophy.
Canadians must be assured that their treatment by public servants will not be coloured by political affiliation, just as

February 9, 1988
Public Employees Political Rights
they must be assured that their treatment is not affected by their sex, their race, their language, or their ethnic origin.
We have laws and regulations prohibiting discrimination on these grounds. However, such regulations do not prohibit people from having bigoted or sexist views, for example, because that of course is impossible, but they do prohibit public servants from manifesting any such views in the execution of their public duties. The same logic is applied in this Bill to the expression of political rights by public servants.
I do not think that there is a pressing need in this day and age to deprive hundreds of thousands of Canadians of their political rights, but if we are to impose such important limitations, Parliament cannot do so lightly. The restrictions on basic political liberties of public servants are more severe in Canada than in most western democracies. In the United States, Great Britain, Australia, France, and Sweden, public servants have the right to free political expression. More important, when there are restrictions on political activity, these are spelled out clearly in law as they are in the United States.
In the United Kingdom there is a clear delineation of political rights for different categories of public servants, running from complete freedom for the largest category in jobs of little or no political sensitivity, to severe restrictions, similar to those that we now have in Canada, for a small group of senior public servants. The British model is one which has been suggested as an option for Canada by the 1979 report of the Special Committee on the Review of Personnel Management and the Merit Principle, known as the D'Avignon report. It also served as a model for the Bill before us today.
As I have told the House on a number of occasions, I find that the D'Avignon approach seemed to provide the best balance possible between the competing principles of a neutral Public Service and individual freedom of expression. Coming to the present law, the sad reality for Canadian public servants is that Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act is worded vaguely, so that it has left the definition of political liberties up to the Public Service Commission. The commission has been notoriously fickle in its interpretation of the Act, permitting political activities in some parts of the country while denying them in others.
Various federal Departments governed by the Act interpret it in different ways, and federal agencies not subject to the Act have also varied in their interpretations, some permitting almost complete political freedom to their employees and others imposing severe restrictions.
Section 32 does not deal with the right to public comment on political issues. Limitations on freedom of expression are imposed largely through policy or regulation by government agencies, not by legislation. The Public Service Staff Relations Board has set stringent limits on freedom of expression by public servants, banning criticism of public policy by ail employees. It has done this even when it can be shown that
public comments do not affect the performance of a public servant's job.
If our commitment to free speech and freedom of expression is anything, then it is not divisible. Neither clear cause nor vague fears, can be the only justification for limiting basic democratic rights in a free country. If those rights must be limited then Parliament must make that decision, after a careful and measured assessment of the genuine need and clear dangers behind such action.
This Bill aims to provide basic democratic rights to public servants. It ensures that it is Parliament that will set out which rights will be curtailed and how this will be done. It will be Parliament that guarantees the public's right to a non-partisan delivery of public services. I would like to outline briefly how this Bill endeavours to achieve those objectives.
The Bill classifies public servants into three categories, based roughly on the political sensitivity of the duties performed. These categories reflect very closely the recommendations of the 1979 D'Avignon report. In my view this classification is essential if we are to perform properly the required balancing act between the principles I referred to earlier and to recognize that those employees who engage in activities that arc more politically sensitive cannot enjoy the same range of liberties as those whose positions do not touch upon policy at all.
The reasons for not granting full political rights to employees in the executive and senior management occupational groups seem quite clear. It would be most inappropriate for our senior public servants to work in an election campaign to defeat the Minister to whom they are providing advice at the time. All political activities, aside from voting, making financial contributions to a Party, being a member of a political Party, attending political meetings, and within certain limits expressing opinions on matters of public interest, would be prohibited to employees in this category. In other words, pretty much the status quo would be maintained for category A employees. The Bill creates a second category wherein access to full political rights would be subject to request and decision by the Public Service Commission, depending on the specific responsibilities of the applicant and the political sensitivity of those duties.
The occupational groups in this category, as suggested in the D'Avignon report, are set out in Clause 1 of the Bill. I hope that the composition of this category will be reviewed closely and carefully in committee. Some Members may feel that D'Avignon included too many classifications. I know that the Public Service Commission has expressed the view that not enough were included.
The commission would be obligated to hold public hearings to determine the limits, if any, to the political rights that will be extended to employees in this category. However, it is
February 9, 1988

important to remember that it will be Parliament that will have the final say on the regime to govern these groups.
Those category B occupational groups are ones in which the duties of the position vary so that neither a blanket denial nor complete political freedom can be supported. They contain positions whose incumbents may quite properly be allowed to take an active part in politics and others whose duties are such that political activity would be inappropriate. In this category, for example, are employees in the commerce group whose duties involve awarding government contracts, employees in the purchasing and supply group who are responsible for awarding contracts, and staffing officers in the personnel administration group who are directly involved in the recruiting of new employees. The House will be asked in committee to consider whether political action by members of such groups might be seen to be incompatible with the exercise of their responsibilities.
1 recognize that the creation of this middle category of public servants is not universally supported. 1 also realize that it makes for a complex and initially somewhat cumbersome and time-consuming process. However, I am convinced, largely based on my understanding of the British experience, that it is a system which is intellectually more supportable than simply dividing the Public Service into two categories-senior managers and others. Attractive as that approach is from the point of view of simplicity and certainty, it does not, in my view, provide quite the right balance between the need for a politically neutral Public Service and the rights of individual public servants.
Employees in all remaining occupational groups, which constitute the vast majority of public servants, would be placed in category C. This will entitle them to full political rights without review by the Public Service Commission, other than requiring a leave of absence without pay upon nomination by a political Party to contest an election. The activities of these employees rarely touch upon policy and political questions. Granting them the rights shared by other Canadians would hardly jeopardize the neutrality of our Public Service and the effective administration of government policy.
In my view we have allowed the present unjust system to go on for much too long. We have all paid a price for it. It is difficult to estimate how many public servants, committed to improving all aspects of life in Canada, have been deterred by the present provisions of the Public Service Employment Act.
This Bill is by no means perfect. Indeed, on rereading it after it was printed I noticed a number of imperfections. I am sure that some of them will be pointed out today. I am also sure that a number of them can be dealt with at committee.
The regime as set out in Bill C-273 is one that I would commend to the House. It sends out the clear message that all Canadians may contribute to political life in our country and that the safeguards for a neutral, non-partisan Public Service will remain in place.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   PUBLIC EMPLOYEES POLITICAL RIGHTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congragulate the Hon. Member for
Public Employees Political Rights
Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney) for introducing this Bill for discussion in the House, and I hope that the House will agree to refer this Bill to a committee this afternoon if necessary. I want to congratulate him on his initiative, because having personally on several occasions debated the issue of extended rights for Federal public servants, especially the right to participate in the political life of this country, I recognize that his initiative provides us with food for thought. I thank him for his well-reasoned remarks concerning Bill C-273.
It is an interesting Bill fashioned after the D'Avignon report, a report which had been commissioned by the Liberal Government of the time concerning the application of the merit principle in the Public Service of Canada.
The Bill is therefore global. It is interesting to note that the Hon. Member has addressed every possible aspect of this issue and provided also not only for more generous application, but also for the review of the issue by a House committee every four years, a suggestion which I feel is new and which I welcome most positively.
The purpose of this Bill is not new. As I was saying earlier, I had an opportunity, on September the 23rd, 1985, to move in the House a motion calling essentially for the same thing. What is new is that a Government member has introduced a Bill which is fairly complete and in my opinion meets almost all of D'Avignon's expectations. I am aware, just as the Hon. Member for Ottawa West is, that this idea originated in the British Parliament, the so-called mother of Parliaments, and 1 feel the matter is important because there are now 200 000 federal civil servants who rather arbitrarily are openly denied their democratic privileges during an election campaign.
Hon. Members will know that, whenever there is an election campaign, the Public Service Commission sends a letter or notice to public servants in which it says: Section 32 of the Act prohibits your active participation in an election, even though, according to our interpretation, you may hold a membership card, make financial contributions, and even attend political meetings, but you cannot be seen or participate actively in a federal campaign as a supporter of one of the political parties. I find this regrettable because, as someone from the National Capital Region, it is quite clear to me that many public servants want to take part in the democratic process, to act according to their political beliefs and to help the candidate of their choice get elected.
It is a secret for no one, Mr. Speaker, that we all have in our constituencies, whether Ottawa-Vanier, Ottawa West, Ottawa Centre or Ottawa Carleton, public servants who work in our election campaigns and who are very helpful to us. It should be clearly understood that legal proceedings can be taken against a public servant only if a candidate in an election lodges a complaint with the Commission saying that a public servant has worked for the election of another person. I must say that no candidate has ever complained in Canada that a public servant has worked for someone else during an election.

February 9, 1988
Public Employees Political Rights
As we all know that there are public servants who work for candidates in political elections, we should put an end to this hypocritical practice of refusing to admit it openly. As for me, I say so quite openly: There are indeed public servants who work for me during election campaigns. I encourage them to continue to do so, because 1 am convinced that, for the majority of them, it is their democratic and constitutional. 1 find it difficult to believe that another candidate in a federal election would object to the participation of a public servant who, according to Mr. D'Avignon's classification or that proposed in the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), belongs to category C and is not in a position to advise the Government of the day. 1 cannot understand how someone could say that a doctor practising medicine, a veterinarian working at the Experimental Farm, or another public servant, whether he is a bookkeeper, a postal worker or an employee of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, might in any way embarrass the Government by taking part in a democratic electoral process.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, when the Canadian Public Service issues its instructions for an election, it gives a very narrow, and to my mind unfair, interpretation of the Act. It is not the responsibility of the Commission to legislate. It is the responsibility of Parliament, but the employer, the Treasury Board, also has the responsibility to suggest and implement changes to modernize the Act and make it reflect the Canadian reality.
Mr. Speaker, during the 1984 electoral campaign, the Conservatives promised that this matter would be settled and that a parliamentary committee would examine the whole issue of the political participation of public servants. We Liberals said that we supported the idea of having a committee of the House discuss and examine this issue. The New Democrats also agree with us. I don't see the problem. The back-benchers agree and I think the Government must act fairly with all its employees. We must eliminate hypocrisy and settle this issue some day. Let's do it today. It is a Government commitment which is supported by the opposition Parties. I don't see where the problem is.
I would like to repeat it, Madam Speaker, I think that today a federal employee who gets involved in a procedure as central to democracy as the election of a Member of Parliament must not be threatened with proceedings if he or she has been identified in the Hon. Member's Bill as a category C employee, whose involvement would not be subject to any limits. I think that it is a good idea to divide employees into three categories: A, B and C. Obviously, those who work at high levels advise the Government. It would not be realistic to allow them to participate in an election campaign in which the Government that they themselves would have advised would be criticized . As for the Category B employees-as I have already said in a speech on September 23, 1985-it is a question of judgment since some public servants occupy
positions where discretionary decisions are taken and they could be accused of favouritism or partisanship.
As for the category C employees, probably 80,000 to 85,000 public servants, I think they could be freed of all restriction and allowed to participate freely in the democratic process.
To conclude, then. Madam Speaker, so that other Hon. Members may have the opportunity to speak, 1 want to say that since it is an administrative step that has to be taken and the House of Commons agrees to free an important number of public servants, let's do it and send the Bill to the committee so that the question can be examined and the decision be taken before the next election to allow many public servants to participate.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   PUBLIC EMPLOYEES POLITICAL RIGHTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted, on behalf of my constituents of Nepean- Carleton, to rise in the House to share some of my thoughts relative to the Private Member's Bill put by the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney) dealing with the political rights of public servants.
I have spoken on this issue in the House several times before, but today I wish to make special reference to my comments of February 7, 1986, at page 10607 of Hansard. 1 would like to quote my remarks from that time so that Hon. Members will know that I have been consistent in my approach to the matter on which I wish to speak this afternoon. This is what I said:
1 personally favour in style the recommendations which were put forward in the D'Avignon Report. It is a concept which is fairly widely used in the British House of Commons and in the British Parliament, where public servants are in fact tiered. For example, there is a tier of persons who have total political freedoms and an upper tier of those who do not.
I would like to compliment my colleague from Ottawa West for raising this issue. I think he has a very sensitive feel for public servants, having been one himself, a very sensitive feel for the handicap the present regulations place upon public servants and a very sensitive feel for finding a constructive solution to this, a solution which he has proposed in his Bill. As well, in this Private Members' Hour, I want to compliment my colleague for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for showing support for this Private Member's Bill, hoping that it will go to a vote this afternoon and from there on to a legislative committee.
There is no question that this item was pivotal in many of the activities associated with the process of the 1984 election. In that process, questions were put to political Parties on their policies, and I shall really only deal with the response given by my Party. The question put was as follows: "Would your Party be prepared to remove the current restrictions on the rights of federal Public Service employees and grant full political rights to employees currently covered by collective agreements?" The response to that was as follows: "The Progressive Conservative
February 9, 1988

Party favours a general removal of the restrictions on political activity, especially for those public servants covered by collective agreements. These restrictions are unnecessary and may not be justifiable under the terms of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. There are some senior public servants whose job responsibilities are very political in nature and whose rights should be somewhat restricted to prevent conflict of interest. But we are confident that these people could be covered separately without disenfranchising over 200,000 public servants in the process." That is the position of my Party and, I presume, the position of the Government.
In the 1984 election public servants operated under a very difficult handicap. A memorandum was issued to all public servants by the Public Service Commission dated February, 1984, under the signature of Edgar Gallant, then Chairman of the Public Service Commission. He outlined the guidelines under which public servants would be expected to operate. To highlight a couple of them let me quote the following: "For greater clarity of this general principle we propose the following guidelines:
First, employees should not personally campaign for or against political parties or candidates in federal, provincial or territorial elections.
Employees should not become involved in the solicitation, collection, distribution or administration of the finances of political parties.
Employees should not assume any official functions.
Employees must not stand for elected office or seek nomination in a federal, provincial or territorial election unless they have first obtained permission from the Public Service Commission to take leave without pay in order to do so."
Those guidelines effectively made political eunuchs out of all public servants. 1 very much regretted that because I spent most of the 1970s in municipal politics where you put together and work with a team of people who help you get elected, provide you with advice on policy matters, and who are generally part of your team. It was disappointing to me as I sought nomination and eventual election to this House that so many people who were part of that team in earlier days felt it necessary not to participate in the federal process and assist someone like myself in seeking higher office. Those people are my friends, neighbours, people I had worked with professionally or touched in other ways and it was really regrettable. However, in that memorandum that I referred to, Mr. Gallant makes this final comment: "Until Parliament gives further manifestations of its will the above constitutes our interpretation of the spirit and scope of the law in regard to the political impartiality of Public Service employees." It is against that background that I am so happy to speak to this Bill before us this afternoon because I find it closely approximates what I supported back on February 7, 1986, and which I believe would be a good way of solving the problem.
Public Employees Political Rights
My colleague suggests in his Bill that public servants be divided into three categories. One category would be those who are responsible for developing policy, policy recommendations and policy advice, and they would be effectively restricted from the political process. The third category, described as category C, would be a person who could participate in depth. Then there is a group in between which would have to go to a judiciary council of some sort to decide whether or not they would have that right.
When you look at this Bill in some detail you will find that it recommends that all public servants have the right to vote, to make financial contributions, to be a member of a political Party, and to attend political meetings. He outlines very thoughtfully as well that no public servant can make a public statement that directly conflicts with the duties of his or her position. That is a very useful item in the Bill. It prevents public servants from commenting on the area in which they work professionally or technically.
The Bill goes on to add in Clause 5 that no category C employee shall engage in an activity during working hours. Those two points, that you are not to comment in any circumstances on your area of professional activity or comment at all during working hours, really safeguard the public in a remarkable way. Those employees who fall into category C are able to work for a candidate, be a candidate, and solicit funds, and hold office.
It is absolutely essential that this Parliament find a solution to enable public servants to participate with good conscience in the political process. I believe this Bill provides that opportunity. The Public Service that ! know is very professional. It includes Departments like Energy, Mines and Resources, Agriculture Canada, and the National Research Council. I am confident they will approach this with a great deal of professionalism. Therefore, I would urge all Hon. Members in the House this afternoon to send this Bill to a legislative committee so that we can move forward with something which is awfully important to a significant number of Canadians.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   PUBLIC EMPLOYEES POLITICAL RIGHTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome Bill C-73 and I congratulate the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney) for having brought it forward. I thank him also for his support of similar legislation which I have proposed three times now during Private Members' Hour over the last three and a half years.
As the Hon. Member said, a decision by this House to send this Bill to committee today would send a clear message to the Government. As it happens, the Party which forms the Government is a Party of which he is a Member, and I regret that the promises of the Progressive Conservatives in 1984 on this issue have so far been honoured in the breach when there was clearly a consensus about the need for action.
What is important now is that this Bill not be talked out, and 1 plead with Hon. Members not to do so. I will be the only spokesperson for my Party. It is in the hands of Progressive

February 9, 1988
Public Employees Political Rights
Conservative Members. If they have particular concerns and there is not time to voice them in this hour, then they can take them to committee. I know the committee considering this matter will be happy to give a full hearing to people who have concerns about it.
While I have certain differences with the specifics of this Bill, both I and my Party certainly endorse it in principle. We believe it is a basis on which one can work in order to bring forward effective legislation to protect political rights.
I have brought forward two Bills. Bills C-231 and C-277, on this subject. I expect to go forward shortly to the Federal Court of Appeal with a case on political rights which 1 launched in July of 1984. It takes a long time to move these things through the courts, and I am personally disappointed that Parliament has not yet had a chance to take the necessary action and have this matter referred to a committee. I recall, a bit wryly if I may say so, that earlier, when I suggested this matter be sent to committee, the response from government Members was that it is going to happen so quickly it would be a delay and waste of time for the House to send it to committee for further study.
My colleague from Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) referred to the promise of the Conservative Party which was quite clear. During the 1984 election campaign the Conservative Party said that the present restrictions on political activity are unnecessary and that the issue could and should be addressed without disenfranchising over 200,000 public servants. There is no question about the clarity of the promise that was made in 1984. In fact, it says here that the Conservative Party favours a general removal of the restrictions on political activity, especially for those public servants who are covered by collective agreements.
Unfortunately, for the last three and a half years the Conservative Government has abdicated this issue to the Public Service Commission, and I am afraid that the commission has gone far beyond its mandate in terms of its interpretation of Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act. I will come to that in a minute.
There are many similarities between the Bill before us and Bill C-231 which I proposed. In particular, they both agree on the need to repeal Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act. In his Bill, the Member for Ottawa West follows quite closely the D'Avignon report, leaving a restricted group of senior officials who would essentially have few political rights, a middle group who may get political rights if that is approved by the Public Service Commission and by the House of Commons, and a large group, the majority, who would have full rights to participate in political campaigns, to be members of political Parties, to stand for office, et cetera, et cetera.
The Bill I proposed also repeals Section 32. It allows for managerial and confidential employees to be excluded subject to approval by Parliament on each category and then gives full
political rights to all the rest including federal employees in agencies, boards, and commissions who are not covered in the Bill proposed by the Member for Ottawa West. In other words, I had proposed a two-tiered system as opposed to the three-tiered system suggested by my friend from Ottawa West.
My problem with the three-tier proposal is that it is somewhat difficult to implement and that a likely result is that many persons who are not in politically sensitive positions would still wind up without political rights because they would find themselves falling into category B. I note that the Conservative Party's promise in 1984 was that it would extend political rights particularly to persons covered by collective bargaining agreements.
However, in fact most members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service would find themselves, according to the Bill of the Member for Ottawa West, in this grey area. They would be people working in such areas as commerce, program manager, purchasing and supply, law, information services, or personnel management. Likewise, members of the economists, sociologists, and statisticians Union all fall within the ESS category, which would also be in that grey area in category B.
I said earlier that I am disappointed that the Government has dragged its feet when there was clearly room for leadership on this particular issue. There have been elections in almost every province since 1984, and the restrictions which have been enforced by the Public Service Commission have applied to federal government employees who might have wished to become involved in those elections. There have been byelections in several provinces; in the Yukon, Quebec, and Newfoundland, since 1984. The restrictions have applied there as well.
The basic problem of the Government's failure to act has really been a failure to endorse the professionalism of people working in the Public Service. The question is whether people working in Government can act impartially in the way in which we would all hope they would act and remove any personal opinions that they may have. As the Member for Ottawa West pointed out, those personal opinions exist whether or not a person is a member of a political Party. No one suggests that public servants fail in general to act impartially despite what their personal views may be. Yet the Government has failed to recognize that by not acting on the question of political rights.
Likewise, as we have seen in the last two weeks with the decision of the Supreme Court on the Charter of Rights, the Supreme Court is taking a strong position in terms of charter freedoms. The Charter guarantees freedom of expression and freedom of association subject to such restrictions as are justifiable in a free and democratic society.
This is the cornerstone of the case which I have before the Federal Court of Appeal, but until the courts finally rule we have a chilling effect which, as my colleague from Nepean has indicated, is particularly strong on Members in the national
February 9, 1988

capital area because of the concentration of federal government employees in this particular area.
I would remind my colleagues that the Ontario Law Reform Commission held a very effective and extensive set of hearings and studies on the issue of political rights for government employees and came up with a position which is very close to that which was proposed in my Bill and in the Bill which we are debating right now as proposed by the Member for Ottawa West.
I would also remind all Members of Parliament that the Public Service Commission is meant to be an agency of Parliament. In fact, however, the articulation, the way by which that commission reports to Parliament, is extremely weak. There is now a Committee on Government Operations to which that commission is meant to report, but it is not called on to account regularly on its activities. When that committee or its predecessor has been critical of the Public Service Commission for its interpretation of Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act, the commission has essentially thumbed its nose at Members of Parliament to whom it is meant to be responsible. I for one, as a Member of Parliament, find that behaviour objectionable and indefensible.
Section 32 of the Act says essentially that public employees should not work for or against a candidate in an election. However, the guidelines issued by the Public Service Commission go far further than that. They state that federal Public Service employees should not undertake activities, assume responsibilities, or make public statements of a politically partisan nature or of a kind which could give rise to the perception that they may not be able to perform their duties as public employees in a politically impartial manner.
As long as Edgar Gallant was the Chairman of the Public Service Commission we knew that his perception was that there was a biased politically partisan public servant under every stone and that the least activity in which they engaged would give, in his view, the perception. In other words, there was no definition of what the perception was all about.
Unfortunately, his successor, Mrs. Huguette Labelle, has taken very much the same position. Although she has acknowledged that the courts and the Federal Court of Appeal have forced the Public Service Commission to climb back on some of its interpretations in law, there has been no effort to circulate that among federal government Departments and federal employees in the active, vigorous, and productive way which was undertaken in February, 1984, when the current guidelines were circulated.
I agree with my colleagues. 1 believe that in five or ten minutes or right now, if you will, we should let this Bill go to committee and allow this matter to have a full airing. If the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) has a Bill, let him bring it forward and send it to the same committee. Let us get action on this issue so that the fundamental rights of public employees are not ignored in the next election as they have been in so many previous elections.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   PUBLIC EMPLOYEES POLITICAL RIGHTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
First of all, Madam Speaker, I should like to congratulate my friend the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney) for putting together Bill C-273 concerning the political rights of public employees.
Madam Speaker, we are called upon today to deal with an issue which is not new but which certainly deserves our undivided attention. As a matter of fact, we have been concerned already for quite some time with the problem of the participation of public employees in political activities as well as their involvement in political associations. Since the beginning of this century, when a number of pieces of legislation were implemented to ensure the neutrality and impartiality of the Federal Public Service, this organization has made every effort to maintain a fair balance between the individual rights of its employees and the collective rights of the Canadian public.
Public Service impartiality is an issue of great concern especially to the Ministers who must be quite sure that the advice they are getting is unbiased and not based on partisan considerations. It is also of great concern to the public employees themselves whose faithfulness, obedience or even opportunities for promotion must not be influenced by the result of a federal election. The importance of this impartiality is reflected in the provisions of the Public Service Employment Act which clearly limit the political activities of federal employees, and 1 quote:
No employee shall engage in work for, on behalf of or against a candidate
for election-or engage in work for, on behalf of or against a political party.
In view of the current legislation, public employees cannot participate actively in the political process, which means for instance that they cannot show their support for a candidate or political party. They may however be a candidate in an election, provided they have been authorized to do so by the Public Service Commission. This permission may be denied if their political involvement were likely to conflict with the impartial and neutral exercise of their duties.
For example, it is obvious that a deputy minister has to avoid any kind of partisan politics in the discharge of his responsibilities. Some other public servants simply must be impartial about government policy. This is why Public Service Commission officials have to keep in mind the employment category and level of a public servant asking for leave to run as a candidate in an election.
The commission wants to make sure that the public will never have any doubt as to the possibility of conflict of interests in the case of the employee involved. Of course civil servants can take passive participation in federal or provincial politics by making contributions to a party or exercising their right to vote.

February 9, 1988
Adjournment Debate
For a few years now some people have been expressing doubts about the legitimacy of restricting public employees to passive participation, particularly by people claiming specific individual rights.
The issue has become more relevant since the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms was proclaimed in 1982. 1 should like to quote the Charter section 2:
Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:
(a)	freedom of conscience and religion;
(b)	freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of
the press and other media of communication;
(c)	freedom of peaceful assembly; and
(d)	freedom of association.
The Charter refers to the fundamental freedoms of all Canadians, and section 3 reads:
Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election of members of
the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly and to be qualified for
membership therein.
However the Charter acknowledges the right to impose reasonable restrictions. So if we accept the principle that public employees must be subject to certain restrictions, these have to be defined.
The Government believes that such restrictions concerning the political activities of public employees should be as few as possible. However, we have to proceed with caution, because it would be unacceptable to compromise the neutrality of the Public Service and to question the principle of a permanent Public Service based on the merit principle, of a Public Service which can serve the Government objectively in the interests of all Canadians.
We have to recognize that, by the very nature of their responsiblities and their work, public servants must maintain some degree of impartiality to protect the integrity of the institution.
Thus, the Government must be assured that its policies will not be openly criticized by its public servants. On the other hand, public servants must remain neutral in the advice they give or the positions they may have to fill. It is indeed for this reason that the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daub-ney) divides public servants into three categories in his Bill. The first includes public servants in the executive and senior management groups, who would be granted limited political rights; the second includes public servants of other professional groups, for whom the Public Service Commission would establish the required restrictions, and the third includes all other public servants, who would be granted extensive political rights.
The Commission has already been the subject of studies, such as that carried out by the Special Committee on the Review of Personnel Management and the Merit Principle, better known as the D'Avignon Committee. In his report, Mr. D'Avignon mentions the British regulatory system, which is based on a categorization of positions according to the nature
of the duties and the extent to which their incumbents are involved in the process of policy-making and of advising the Government. According to Mr. D'Avignon, this system would be an excellent example to follow for the Canadian Public Service. Employees in a position which is not defined as being of a sensitive nature have full freedom to be politically active, while those who hold a sensitive position are denied the right to play an active role in politics.
It is difficult but not impossible to find a proper balance between exercising the rights of all Canadian citizens and maintaining the principle of neutrality of the Canadian Public Service. While recognizing the risks of giving back their political rights to public servants, we have to ensure that the restrictions imposed on them are not unreasonable.
Madam Speaker, others will have their own opinions on the best way to achieve a proper balance, and I shall listen carefully to their comments during this debate.

Madam Speaker, I know that you are a very busy person and do not have an opportunity to watch very much television. I wonder if, on occasion, you have seen the program called The Great White Northl You may think that today, here in Ottawa, that is exactly what it is, but that is not what 1 am talking about.
The program that I am talking about is the one with a couple of characters named the MacKenzie brothers. Do you not recognize Bob and Doug MacKenzie? Perhaps if I use the phrase "Take off, eh", that may ring a bell.
As you know, on that program they seem to consume quite a bit of alcoholic refreshment known as beer. I do not know whether the beer they are consuming is Labatt, Molson,
February 9, 1988

Carling or O'Keefe, but I do know if Bob and Doug MacKenzie are consuming that beer here in Ottawa, Ontario or Quebec, they are not consuming Moosehead beer.
Moosehead beer may not mean anything to you, but Moosehead beer is made in New Brunswick and can be bought in New Brunswick. It can be bought in Nova Scotia, as the Flon. Parliamentary Secretary knows. I am told that you can even buy it in the United States. In fact, it is the fourth most popular brand of some 400 brands of beer that are imported into the United States. Strangely enough, one cannot buy Moosehead beer here in Ottawa, nor in Quebec. In fact, one cannot buy it anywhere in Canada except in New Brunswick or in Nova Scotia.
You probably do not care, Madam Speaker. If you drink beer at all, you may drink another brand, or you may not drink it at all, and I am sure you probably do not. However, do you not think it is strange and peculiar that we cannot get Moosehead beer here in Ottawa?
The reason we cannot get Moosehead beer in Ontario is because of something called "interprovincial trade barriers". As you know, Madam Speaker, the Government has negotiated a trade agreement with the United States to help reduce the trade barriers between Canada and the United States. As well, we are in the midst of trying to negotiate through the GATT to reduce trade barriers around the world. However, for some reason or other, we still have these trade barriers right here in Canada which affect a great many products, not just Moosehead beer.
There is a vast array of examples of these interprovincial trade barriers. Back in 1985, the Quebec Government ordered the City of Aylmer, Quebec, to rip up a street that was paved with bricks because those bricks were made in Ontario. It ordered the city to replace those bricks with bricks made in Quebec. In addition, I am told New Brunswick has a surplus of fish processing capacity and Newfoundland has a surplus of fish but they cannot get together because of these trade barriers.
Ontario keeps milk produced in Quebec out of the province. Quebec prohibits the export of timber that is not fully processed in Quebec. British Columbia, I am told, has a markup of 50 per cent on British Columbia wine, while it has a mark-up of 110 per cent on Ontario or Quebec wine. Ontario will not even sell Quebec wine or British Columbia wine. As you can see, Madam Speaker, there is a vast array of these trade barriers.
One of the worst trade barriers, I suppose, is the purchasing preferences of provincial Governments, and I might say it is not just provincial Governments. They often give a preference of a 5 per cent or 10 per cent additional price to a supplier in their own province rather than buying it at a cheaper price from a supplier in another province. I am very familiar with that situation because when I served as a hydro commissioner
Adjournment Debate
in Metropolitan Toronto, we gave a 5 per cent purchasing preference to local firms. The reason we did that is because the chairman of the Hydro Commission, an excellent fellow by the name of Jack Christie, who had served for years and years, became a little upset that our local suppliers were discriminated against elsewhere and insisted that we discriminate as well against suppliers from other parts of the country. Therefore, I am very familiar with this kind of trade barrier.
1 am told that 20 per cent of Canadian manufacturers have difficulty selling their goods in other parts of Canada because of these trade barriers. What can we do about all of this? The Government has been trying to do something about it, to its credit. In 1985 the Government set up a task force on interprovincial trade which is co-chaired by the federal Director General of DRIE and the Deputy Minister of Economic Development in the Province of Alberta. That is aimed at attempting to get rid of interprovincial trade barriers.
At the First Ministers Conference held last November in Toronto, and 1 was present at that time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Premiers set up a committee of Ministers to deal with the question of internal trade, and to try to improve the situation. In addition, the federal Government has appointed Mr. Jim Grandy, a former federal bureaucrat, to attempt to reduce the trade barriers in areas like purchasing preferences, and also for beer, wine, and liquor.
We have a lot of committees, Madam Speaker, but what we need now is some action. It would be a shame if we got rid of the trade barriers between Canada and the United States, and got rid of the trade barriers with Canada and other parts of the world, but somehow or other at the same time we had those internal trade barriers.
Tonight, 1 would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary to assure us that he, the Minister, and the Government will get rid of those interprovincial trade barriers. I am going to ask him to tell us the progress that they have made. I am going to ask him to ensure, to the use the words of the MacKenzie brothers, that we tell the interprovincial trade barriers to "Take off, eh!"
Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for
Science and Technology): Madam Speaker, we have taken off in the reduction of barriers to interprovincial trade. I might say to my dear friend that one can buy Moosehead beer in Texas.
I know that.

Very shortly one will be able to buy Moosehead beer in British Columbia, and here in Ontario. No other Government has been more concerned about the impediments caused to

February 9, 1988

trade in Canada by artificial barriers, provincial barriers, than has this Government.
Domestically such barriers remain a great hindrance to trade, and a great hindrance to the development of our competitive capacity. We want to get rid of them once and for all. We must encourage Canadians to become competitive nationally and internationally. One of the ways we do it best is in the reduction and elimination, which is the ideal goal, of many of those barriers.
