speechtext:
Madam Speaker. I am rising this evening to continue discussion on a question regarding the Government's unwarranted and unprecedented interference with the decision of the CRTC to award the allnews licence to the CBC.
Canadians are concerned about the Government's intervention into the decision of the CRTC; it was a fair and open decision-making procedure. This intervention challenges its authority, its process, its decision making and its autonomy.
The CRTC decision was taken after long deliberations and after weeks of public hearings with support from every province, with the exception of P.E.I., and the three major cable system operators-Rogers, Western Cable Systems, and Telecable Laurentien. The CRTC decision was based upon the CBC's proven ability to best manage such a service. Previous calls for such an all-news service had been made. Only one other applicant showed interest. It was based on merit. The CBC offered the best service and the most complete Canadian content. The licence was won by the CBC because its proposal was far superior.
The CBC had openly indicated its interest in rendering such a service to the Caplan-Sauvageau task force on broadcasting policy which widely consulted Canadians and recommended this service. Some $2.9 million was spent by the task force to come out and say: "We think this is a good idea for Canadians''. Then our Standing Committee on Communications and Culture studied and tabled an extensive report on speciality services and never objected to such a licence. The Chairman never objected to such a licence. The Minister appeared before the committee and never indicated any concern in respect of the CBC, and she was well aware of its proposal. She never challenged the arm's length right of the CBC board to take such a decision. There was an appropriate time and place for the Minister to make a policy statement or quietly inform the CBC that its request was not in her interest or in her view; that would have been an acceptable request. To come in after the fact is totally reprehensible.
The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) has said that Cabinet cannot make a final decision on the licence until September 1, when the CBC licence is officially awarded by the CRTC. This causes us all grave concern. Why? It is because of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is reported as having said following the CRTC decision on allnews. 1 will quote what he supposedly said:
There is no way this Government is going to allow that flawed decision to
stand. Instead of hammering us two hours a day, they will be hammering us 24
hours a day.
I believe these statements are prejudicial to a fair Cabinet review.
If the Tory Cabinet decided to succumb to the pressures of the "Back-Benchers Club" or the BBC, it will be a precedent. Never before has Cabinet taken such an action against the CRTC. What credibility and impression will future decisions have? What damage has been done?
How can a government pressure the CBC to find a private sector partner, which it had already tried to do but people were not interested because they did not see enough profit potential in the particular project? How can a government ask the CBC to provide an equivalent service in the French language, which it had already planned to do and a feasibility study was already in progress, after such a service has been awarded? That amounts to changing the rules in the middle of the game. I do not believe that this is fair, and the Canadian public does
February 9, 1988

not think that it is fair. What kind of message is the Government sending? Is it telling Canadians that it only believes in fair competition when the winner is who it wants? How does this affect the image of the CRTC? What about its credibility? What about the credibility of the CBC board and arm's length?
It has been suggested that the CBC all-news service will result in unnecessary concentration of news influence. Canadians do not want concentration, particularly in news, but this was just a smoke and mirrors argument to deflect the interference and the pressure by the backroom boys. This service will not be concentration in the market. The CRTC secretariat showed that as of March 31, 1987, there are 602 originating radio stations and 104 originating television stations operating in Canada, all of which are privately owned. The CBC has 16 outlets.
In addition, there are 110 daily newspapers, 1,277 weekly or community newspapers and 14 news services all privately owned. How can this be concentration?
At present, the American CNN provides 24-hour cable news in Canada. By the Government's action it is allowing American concentration and an American monopoly to exist in our specialty services. In an area crucial to the forming of a Canadian perspective reflecting Canadian culture and values and our sovereign approach to international issues, as well as understanding regional diversity and concerns from all parts of Canada, this service, 70 per cent of which was to be produced outside of central Canada, is seriously needed. The CBC with its infrastructure in place was the obvious best choice. What Canadians deserve is the best choice, not the biased choice of the Government. The CBC is targeting for 1 per cent of the audience share, which is clearly enunciated in its proposal. I would not call that concentration.
With respect to French language service, the Minister of Communications on behalf of the Government expressed concerns about the appropriateness of embarking upon a major expansion of news and information program services in one official language. However, one of the conditions of the CBC licence was to complete a feasibility study for such a service.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister's attempt to be noble is rather shallow when she talks about insisting on this French all-news service. To consider an equivalent French language service the Government should have announced funds to fulfil such a mandate. It knows perfectly well that the market is smaller with respect to providing a profit so that there will be a requirement to subsidize from the English side or from the Government. What private sector company will become involved in providing a service when there will be no profit?
If the CBC makes the changes that the Government desires then it will fail to meet the terms of its present mandate. This will probably require the CRTC to call for new applications
Adjournment Debate
and for new hearings to be held. Another year will be lost. This will allow the American CNN to gain more and more of a foothold in the Canadian market.
Is this what Canadians want? I do not think so. The Minister has not articulated any clear vision about the future of Canadian TV other than to tell us that we need to hear each other's stories. The Government of the Prime Minister has certainly interfered in such an opportunity. It is communication through direct dictatorship.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROPOSED ALLNEWS TELEVISION CHANNEL-SUGGESTED PARTNERSHIP WITH PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) has characterized the position of the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) on the CBC's news and information service as a request for a "shotgun wedding" between the corporation and the private sector.
I would like to clarify this matter by repeating here in this House just what the Minister of Communications did say in her letter to the President of the CBC on this subject. I quote:
My colleagues and 1 have identified two major areas of concern arising from
the CRTC decision respecting the CBC news and information service. They
are:
1)	The degree to which the proposed licence might contribute to excessive concentration in the field of news programming. This concern might be addressed by an alternative service embracing both the private and public sectors of the Canadian Broadcasting System.
2)	The appropriateness of embarking upon a major expansion of news and information program services in one official language without simultaneously addressing the requirements of the other official language group.

Mr. Speaker, we believe that co-operation between the private and public sectors is possible.
For example, I would like to remind the hon. Member that the CTRC responded favourably to the TV5 application. It involves a consortium composed of eight Canadian organizations:
Three public broadcasters: the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; the Societe de Radio-Television du Quebec and the Ontario Educational Communications Authority.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, the minister of Communications has simply stated publicly that the Government has concerns that it will consider when the issue is brought forward in the autumn for formal review.
In view of these concerns, and the possibility of further petitions to the Governor in Council between now and next October, the Government feels it would not be prudent for the CBC to undertake major expenditures or structural reorganization to implement the proposed service at this time.
Some of the largest French-language private broadcasting undertakings include Tele-Metropole Inc., Cogego Inc.,

February 9, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Television Quatre-Saisons Inc., the National Film Board of Canada and the firm Film Sat Inc. representing Quebec's independent producers.
The Government believes that for the news and information service, the CBC could use the period until October to examine approaches such as a partnership drawing on the skills and resources of the private sector as well as its extensive newsgathering services already deployed.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROPOSED ALLNEWS TELEVISION CHANNEL-SUGGESTED PARTNERSHIP WITH PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some 15 months ago, I brought to the attention of the then Minister of State for Science and Technology the fact that the Government's program for scientific research and development had led to the virtual termination of the world-class astronomical observatory at Algonquin Park. In trying to explain what was happening, the then Minister said:
-what the Prime Minister has indicated in his book, and what I have
repeated many times is that we will spend as much as is necessary to position
Canada and its industries in the new frontier effectively and in every possible
way.
We are now three years into a Conservative Government and what do we see? When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) was the Leader of the Official Opposition, he castigated the Liberal Government by saying, and quite correctly, that among the OECD countries and Japan, Canada had one of the poorest records in efforts and expenditures for scientific research and development. He pointed out that in those years, we were allocating substantially less than 2 per cent of our Gross National Product to scientific research and development and he promised that a Conservative Government would more than double that quickly so that we would spend about 2.5 per cent of our Gross National Product on scientific research and development.
After three years of a Conservative Government, the Prime Minister had to admit at a recent scientific conference that in the last year, we had only devoted 1.3 per cent of our Gross National Product to scientific research and development. Why did that happen? It happened because the Conservative Government is locked into its ideological belief that somehow, if we were to just let the free enterprise system operate, it will do better than any Government effort.
The Government has tried to persuade the private sector to increase dramatically its expenditures. That has not happened. After three years of Conservative Government, we are now doing even worse than we did when the Liberals were in office.
At a recent conference, the Prime Minister promised that the Government would allocate new money, $250 million per year for the next five years, for research in universities. Even if that takes place and if the attempt to persuade the private sector to increase its efforts in the field of scientific research and development were to work, which it has not up until now, and if the Government matches those increases, we will still
have only marginally increased the funding for the granting council.
What has been the result? We can read about it in newspaper accounts of the last few days. Yesterday's Winnipeg Free Press carried a story entitled "Morale weaker at NRC". The story says:
The parking lots at National Research Council laboratories aren't full on
Saturdays any more-
"Morale is certainly not what it used to be at NRC," says Herzberg,-
That is Gerhard Herzberg, one of the few Canadian scientists whose efforts have led to a Nobel Prize.
The union representing most of the scientists, the Professional Institute, issued a statement which was reported in today's Ottawa Citizen. The institute said that federal government laboratories need stable funding and better management and pointed out that the Government should stop budget cuts in federal research establishments and not privatize federal laboratories for purely ideological reasons.
Again, yesterday we learned that the head of the space agency has resigned. Why? Because the Government, after months of argument apparently, cannot even decide where the space agency head office should be. In December of 1987 the Minister said it was critical that the agency head office be in place early this year. Now, obviously because Ministers are still fighting about whether it should be in Ottawa or Montreal, the same Minister says it is no longer critical. A story in today's Citizen says:
Today, the space industry is frustrated and government workers designated
as part of the new agency are in limbo.
Its head, Art Collin, has resigned, saying his job of drafting the required
legislation and finding staff was finished iong ago.
We need to have the Government live up to the commitments the Prime Minister made before the election and do what is needed to make this country prosperous and have its people working in the next 10 to 20 years. We need to raise our efforts in the field of scientific research and development so that we will at least come close to what other western industrialized countries are doing. The time when we could continue complacently to lag far behind those countries has long since passed.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROPOSED ALLNEWS TELEVISION CHANNEL-SUGGESTED PARTNERSHIP WITH PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the Hon. Member has asked us during the late show to talk about the subject concerning his question, and he lost no time in making other comments on our science and technology policy.
Since he asked a question concerning the closing down of the Observatory, I shall give him the information I have, and then I shall set a few facts straight. The Hon. Member's statement reflects a blatant lack of understanding about the major
February 9, 1988

initiatives taken by the Federal Government for the progress of science and technology in Canada.
In 1986, the Hon. Member had already raised the question of the closing down of the Algonquin Observatory. However, following the steps taken by the Government, Canadian scientists obtained access to the most sophisticated astrophysi-cal facilities in the world, namely the giant telescope of James Clerk Maxwell in Hawaii. Canadian scientists, from coast to coast, totally support the present situation.
For the time being, no other decision has been made and the facility will stay in operation this winter, and other decisions could be made next Summer.
Contrary to what is mentioned in several reports and questions, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) has played no part in the budget cuts concerning the Algonquin radioastronomical Observatory. The management of the NRC made this decision after consultation with the representatives of the astronomy community in Canada. Therefore, we assume that these people have advised according to what they thought was in the best interest of the Canadian astronomical community under the current conditions.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make the following observation. Since the Conservative Party was elected in 1984, ever since we have formed the Government, our policy with regard to science and technology has been a long-term policy and each
Adjournment Debate
of our moves is of extreme importance for the future of the country.
Let us start, if you wish, with the creation of a Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology where people can be heard, where Hon. Members can make suggestions and where Opposition Members can participate in the definition of a strong policy and the building of a larger vision of science and technology.
Let us talk also of the federal-provincial agreements which have been signed. The Cabinet, federal and provincial Ministers work together, because we also promised Canadians that we would introduce new policies after consultation with the provinces and in a spirit of mutual understanding.
We also, Mr. Speaker, authorized new funding. By God, Mr. Speaker, it would take me at least an hour to explain everything the Government has done, because it is not just a question of money, it is also a question of long-term strategy. Each of our moves, each of our policies has a bearing on the future of all Canadians.
Next time, Mr. Speaker, I will be able to expand on this subject.
